Yalova'da hayatını kaybeden şarkıcı Güllü'nün ölümüne ilişkin davada yeni deliller TÜBİTAK'a gönderildi. Avukat Rahmi Çelik'in Yalova Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığına yaptığı başvuru üzerine gerekli yazışmaların yapıldığı ve delillerin teknik inceleme için TÜBİTAK'a iletildiği öğrenildi.
'Güllü' adıyla tanınan şarkıcı Gül Tut, 26 Eylül 2025 tarihinde Yalova'nın Çınarcık ilçesi Harmanlar Mahallesi'ndeki evinin penceresinden düşerek hayatını kaybetmişti. Olayla ilgili yürütülen yargılama sonucunda Yalova 1. Ağır Ceza Mahkemesi, 9 Ekim 2026 tarihinde Tuğyan Ülkem Gülter'i üst soya karşı kasten öldürme suçundan ağırlaştırılmış müebbet hapis cezasına çarptırmıştı.
Güllü'nün ölümüyle ilgili Tuğberk Yağız Gülter'in avukatı Rahmi Çelik'in Yalova Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığına yaptığı başvuru kapsamında dosyaya sunulan yeni delillerin TÜBİTAK'a gönderildiği belirtildi. Kasten öldürme suçuna iştirakten Sultan Nur Ulu ve Emin Kervanoğlu hakkında yapılan suç duyurusuna dayanak olarak sunulan deliller TÜBİTAK tarafından incelenecek.
Dosyada daha önce Güllü'nün oğlu Tuğberk Yağız Gülter'in avukatları tarafından ev içi güvenlik kamerası görüntüleri ve ses kayıtlarına ilişkin iki ayrı uzman raporu hazırlatılmıştı. 28 Ekim 2026 tarihli ilk rapor ile 6 Kasım 2026 tarihli ikinci raporda, Güllü'ye atfedilen "Bırak beni" ve "Bırak", Sultan Nur Ulu'ya atfedilen "At", Tuğyan Ülkem Gülter'e atfedilen "Atla camdan" ve "Koş annem yok koş" ifadelerine yer verilmişti. İkinci raporda Tuğyan Ülkem Gülter'e atfedilen "Ben kapattım kameraları" ve "Nasıl yapacağımı düşünüyorum" sözleri de dikkat çekmişti.
Uzman raporlarında kamera kayıtlarında erkek sesi olduğu belirtilen konuşmalar da yer aldı. İlk raporda erkek sesine atfedilen "Sence korkutmaya mı çalışıyor?", "Kapıyı kapat", "Şeref yok" ve "Atsın" ifadeleri aktarılırken, ikinci raporda "Hayır", "Görmek istemiyorum" ve "Atla camdan" sözlerine yer verildi.
Ancak raporlarda erkek sesinin kime ait olduğuna ilişkin kesin bir tespit yapılmadı. İkinci uzman görüşünde ses kayıtlarının olayın aydınlatılması açısından önemli olduğu, ancak tek başına olayın kesin oluş biçimini ortaya koyamayacağı belirtildi.
Güllü'nün ablası Kader Tut'un avukatları Hasan Kocabey ve Şermin Tankut tarafından Bursa Bölge Adliye Mahkemesi ilgili ceza dairesine gönderilmek üzere Yalova 1. Ağır Ceza Mahkemesine sunulan ek beyanda, olay sırasında dairede başka bir kişinin bulunup bulunmadığının araştırılması istendi.
Dilekçede, olay sırasında evde kullanılan telefonlar üzerinden üçüncü kişilerle sesli veya görüntülü görüşme yapılıp yapılmadığının tespit edilmesi talep edildi. Bu kapsamda görüşmeye katılan kişilerin, kullanılan telefonların, cihazların ve uygulama hesaplarının belirlenmesi, daraltılmış baz kayıtlarının incelenmesi ve dijital veriler üzerinde karşılaştırmalı teknik inceleme yapılması istendi.

Türkiye ve Suriye'nin farklı üniversitelerinde görev yapan deprem uzmanları, Maden Tetkik ve Arama Genel Müdürlüğü ile AFAD Deprem ve Risk Azaltma Genel Müdürlüğü yetkilileri, Suriye'deki fay hatlarının bulunduğu bölgelerde çalışmalara başladı.
Türkiye ekibinde AFAD Deprem ve Risk Azaltma Genel Müdürü Prof. Dr. Orhan Tatar koordinatörlüğünde yürütülen çalışmaya Dokuz Eylül Üniversitesi Deprem Araştırma ve Uygulama Merkezi Müdürü Prof. Dr. Hasan Sözbilir, Eskişehir Osmangazi Üniversitesinden Prof. Dr. Volkan Karabacak ve MTA'dan Hasan Elmacı katıldı.
Ölü Deniz Fayı ile bağlantılı bir kısmı Türkiye'de yer alan Yesemek, Hacıpaşa ve Reyhanlı fayları ile Suriye topraklarındaki Afrin, Sarmada ve Armanaz fayları ekipler tarafından incelendi.
Çalışmalara katılan AFAD Deprem Bilim Kurulu Üyesi Prof. Dr. Hasan Sözbilir, AA muhabirine, Türkiye ve Suriye arasında depremsellik ve fayların tanınması için çok kapsamlı çalışma başlatıldığını söyledi.
6 Şubat depremlerinde Türkiye tarafındaki fayların önemli bir kısmının kırıldığını hatırlatan Sözbilir, "Asrın felaketi sonrası komşumuz Suriye'deki sınır ötesi faylarda henüz bir kırılma gerçekleşmedi. Dolayısıyla bu fayların tarih öncesi deprem geçmişini ortaya koymak için bir çalışma yaptık. Öncelikle Afrin, Armanaz ve Sarmada fayları üzerinde arazide inceleme yaptık. Oradaki fayların özelliklerine göre farklı kesimlerinde hendek yerlerini belirledik. Bir sonraki gelişimizde bu faylar üzerinde belli ölçeklerde hendek açacağız. Böylece gelecekte ve yakın dönemde bu fayların depremselliğini ortaya koymuş olacağız." diye konuştu.
Sözbilir, deprem ve yer bilimi konusunda uzman isimlerle Suriye'de 5 gün boyunca fayları incelediklerini dile getirdi.
Fayların bir kısmının Türkiye'den geçtiğini belirten Sözbilir, şunları kaydetti:
"Yarısı bizim tarafta, yarısı Suriye'de olan faylar var. Kilis'ten güneye doğru inen faylar var. Bunlar Ölü Deniz Fayı'nın segmentleri aslında. Ölü Deniz Fay zonu, Kahramanmaraş'tan başlayıp Kızıldeniz'e kadar uzanan yaklaşık 1000 kilometre uzunluğundaki bir fay. Bu fayların önemli bir bölümü 500 ila 2000 yıldır kırılmamış görünüyor. Dolayısıyla bizim için yakın gelecekte kırılma tehlikesi olan faylar hangileri bunları bilmek istiyoruz. Bu faylar son depremi ne zaman yaptı? Ne kadar vaktimiz var, tüm bunları öğrenmek istiyoruz. Türkiye ve Suriye arasındaki faylar bu şekilde ilk kez inceleniyor. Fayları bilimsel olarak tanımaya çalışıyoruz."
AFAD'ın belirleyeceği takvime göre yeniden bölgeye gideceklerini dile getiren Prof. Dr. Sözbilir, yerinde gözlem yaptıkları her fay üzerinde en az ikişer hendek yeri saptadıklarını ifade etti.
20-30 metre eninde ve 3-4 metre derinliğinde hendekler açacaklarını anlatan Sözbilir, "Fayın geçmişini göreceğiz, örnekler toplayacağız, onlar analize gidecek. Elde edeceğimiz verilere göre fayların eski depremlere ait kayıtlarını ortaya çıkaracağız. Tüm bunların ardından bölgedeki fayların Suriye ve Türkiye için ne kadar tehlike oluşturacağı belirlenmiş olacak." diye konuştu.

Amazon MGM Studios'un 16 Kasım'da yaptığı duyuruyla Daniel Craig'in ardından James Bond'u Robert Pattinson canlandıracak. Harry Potter serisindeki Cedric Diggory'den Gotham'ın Batman 'ine uzanan Pattinson'ın 007 olması sosyal medyada büyük ilgi gördü ve seçime gelen yorumların büyük bölümü olumlu oldu.
Robert Pattinson'ın adı geniş kitlelerce ilk kez 2005'te Harry Potter ve Ateş Kadehi'nde canlandırdığı Cedric Diggory ile duyuldu, ardından Alacakaranlık serisindeki Edward Cullen rolüyle dünya çapında yıldızlığa yükseldi. Sonraki yıllarda bağımsız sinemada seçtiği zorlu karakterlerle gençlik idolü imajından sıyrılan oyuncu, Matt Reeves'in The Batman filminde Bruce Wayne'e hayat verdi ve devam filmi The Batman Part II hâlen çekim aşamasında.
Oyuncunun 007'ye uzanan yolunda adını en çok duyuran yapımlar arasında Harry Potter, Alacakaranlık ve The Batman'in yanı sıra Christopher Nolan'ın The Odyssey'i ile Dune serisi de yer alıyor:
• Harry Potter ve Ateş Kadehi: Cedric Diggory • Alacakaranlık (Twilight) serisi: Edward Cullen • The Batman: Bruce Wayne / Batman • The Odyssey: Antinous • Dune: Part Three: Face Dancer • James Bond: 007
Pattinson, Dune: Part Three'de Bond'un yeni yönetmeni Denis Villeneuve ile de çalıştı. Yapımcılar Amy Pascal ve David Heyman da açıklamalarında oyuncunun cesur oyunculuğunu, kendine yönelik esprili tavrını ve kendini yeniden keşfetme becerisini öne çıkardı.
1962'de Dr. No ile başlayan serinin kahramanını Pattinson'dan önce Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan ve Daniel Craig canlandırdı; Pattinson de böylece Bond'u oynayan yedinci isim oldu. Craig, 2006'daki Casino Royale ile başlayan Bond dönemini 2021'de vizyona giren No Time to Die ile kapatmış, filmin finalinde karakter hayatını kaybetmişti.
Seri bu arada el değiştirdi: Amazon 2022'de MGM'i satın aldı, Mart 2025'te Barbara Broccoli ve Michael G. Wilson ile kurulan ortaklık sayesinde Bond'un yaratıcı kontrolünü eline aldı. Yeni 007 arayışında Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Henry Cavill, Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Jacob Elordi, Harris Dickinson, Tom Holland, Josh O'Connor ve Jonathan Bailey gibi çok sayıda isim basında aday olarak anıldı. Sonunda Amazon MGM'in kısa listesinden çıkan isim Pattinson oldu ve film , senaryosunu Steven Knight'ın yazdığı serinin 26. macerası olarak Denis Villeneuve'ün yönetmenliğinde çekilecek.
Amazon MGM'in duyurusunun ardından Pattinson'ın adı sosyal medyada hızla gündeme oturdu. Oyuncu yaptığı açıklamada Bond'un sinemanın en efsanevi karakterlerinden biri olduğunu belirterek rolün kendisine emanet edilmesini hayatının onuru olarak tanımladı; Villeneuve ise Pattinson'ın 007'nin zamansız ruhuna sahip olduğunu söyledi. Seçime gelen tepkilerden bazıları aşağıda yer alıyor.

Bekleyiş sonunda sona erdi ve artık bir sonraki James Bond'un kim olduğunu biliyoruz.
2021 yapımı No Time To Die filminde Daniel Craig'in (hayli kalıcı) veda performansının ardından yıllarca süren spekülasyonların sonrasında, yedinci 007'yi Robert Pattinson canlandıracak .
İngiliz oyuncu, bu çok arzulanan rol için Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, Josh O'Connor, Nicholas Hoult ve Jacob Elordi gibi isimleri geride bıraktı ve Bond olarak seçilen muhtemelen şimdiye kadarki en ünlü oyuncu oluyor.
Sonuç? Aynı anda hem ilham verici, hem sinir bozucu, hem de oldukça güvenli bir tercih.
Her şeyden önce Pattinson, bugün çalışmakta olan en ilginç ve en çok yönlü A-list yıldızlardan biri olduğu söylenebileceği için 007 için akıllıca bir seçim.
Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire ve Twilight serisindeki çıkış rollerinden bu yana, artık 40 yaşında olan İngiliz yıldız, sadece gençlik idoli olmadığını kanıtlamak için çok çalıştı.
Projelerini ve yönetmenlerini akıllıca seçerek David Cronenberg ( Cosmopolis ), James Gray ( The Lost City of Z ), Claire Denis ( High Life ), Robert Eggers ( The Lighthouse ), Safdie kardeşler ( Good Time ), Bong Joon Ho ( Mickey 17 ), Lynne Ramsay ( Die My Love ) ve Christopher Nolan ( Tenet , The Odyssey ) gibi büyük isimlerle çalıştı. Tüm bu filmler, Pattinson'ın bukalemunu andıran, zaman zaman da eksantrik bir ekran varlığı olduğunu ve açıkça her role girebilecek oyunculuk yeteneğine sahip bulunduğunu gösterdi.
2026'yı ele alalım; Pattinson için başarıların ardı ardına geldiği bir yıl oldu: The Drama , The Odyssey , Primetime ... Üstelik henüz Dune: Part Three 'ü izlemedik bile; ki filmin yönetmeni, adı henüz açıklanmayan Bond 26'yı da yöneten Denis Villeneuve.
Bu etkileyici kariyer geçmişiyle, Pattinson'ın Bond'u kendine özgü kılıp rolü kusursuzca oynaması için her türlü şans mevcut.
Bununla birlikte, oyuncu seçimindeki "sinir bozucu" kısma geçelim: Pattinson bu rol için fazla mı nitelikli ve bir başkasına şans vermek güzel olmaz mıydı? Sonuçta kendisi zaten bir megastar, hâlâ mevcut Bruce Wayne / Batman ve The Batman Part II 'nin çekimleri hâlâ devam ediyor...
Kara Şövalye'yi oynayan bir oyuncu aynı zamanda James Bond da olabilir mi? Özellikle Bond rolünün, bugüne kadar hep yıldızı yaratmış bir rol olduğu ve tersine örneklerin pek görülmediği düşünülürse, bu biraz fazla gibi geliyor.
Sean Connery Bond'dan önce görece bilinmeyen bir isimdi; George Lazenby birkaç reklam dışında hiç oyunculuk yapmamıştı; Roger Moore, The Saint sayesinde evlere girmiş bir isimdi ama büyük perdede büyük bir çıkış yakalamamıştı; Timothy Dalton güçlü bir sahne kariyerine sahipti ancak yerleşik bir sinema yıldızı değildi; Pierce Brosnan yıllarca Bond için güçlü bir aday olarak görülmüştü ama aynı adlı TV dizisinde Remington Steele rolüyle tanınıyordu... Daniel Craig'in ise Road To Perdition , Layer Cake ve Munich gibi filmlerde akılda kalan sinema rolleri vardı... Ancak onu gerçek anlamda bir başrol oyuncusuna dönüştüren film Casino Royale oldu.
Buna kıyasla Pattinson, hâlihazırda güvenilir ve gişede sağlam bir başrol oyuncusu; hâlâ kanıtlayacak çok şeyi olan, ancak büyük bir gişe çekim gücü olduğunu da şimdiden ortaya koymuş bir A-list yıldız.
Ve bununla birlikte, Robert Pattinson'ın son derece güvenli bir tercih olduğu gerçeği geliyor.
Bond 26, Amazon'un uzun yıllar seriyi yürüten yapımcılar Barbara Broccoli ve Michael G. Wilson'dan bayrağı devralmasından bu yana çekilen ilk Bond macerası olacak ve şirketin, Bond'un bu yeni döneminde işi ehline verdiklerini kanıtlaması gerekiyor.
Eski kurala göre Pattinson seçilmezdi. Daha yükselişte olan bir oyuncu tercih edilirdi. Pattinson'ın seçilmesi bize Amazon'un risk almaya niyeti olmadığını gösteriyor; paralarının karşılığını fazlasıyla almak istiyorlar ve, tıpkı ondan önce gelen Skyfall gibi, bir sonraki Bond filminin 1 milyar dolarlık bir gişe başarı öyküsü olmasını açıkça hedefliyorlar. Pattinson'ın seçimi ve yönetmen tercihi göz önüne alındığında bunun gerçekleşme ihtimali de oldukça yüksek.
Gerçekten de Denis Villeneuve, hiç kuşkusuz bir Bond filmi üstlenen şimdiye kadarki en heyecan verici yönetmen. Oscar adayı sinemacı henüz kötü bir film çekmedi: Incendies 'den Prisoners 'a, Sicario 'dan Arrival 'a, Blade Runner 2049 'dan Frank Herbert'in sözde filme uyarlanamaz Dune kitaplarını bu neslin Star Wars'u hâline getirmeye uzanan filmografisiyle, en ufak bir tökezleme işareti göstermeyen bir isim.
Bir de Bond 26'nın, Eastern Promises ve Locke 'un senaristi, Peaky Blinders , Taboo , SAS: Rogue Heroes ve The Veil 'in yaratıcısı / yazarı Steven Knight tarafından kaleme alındığını ekleyin; ortaya neredeyse kesin bir gişe başarısı tarifi çıkıyor.
Beklentiler bu kadar göklere çıkmışken, bir sonraki Bond filminin gerçekten gerekeni sunması gerekecek ve Bond rolü beraberinde, az bile söylersek, hatırı sayılır bir inceleme ve sorgulamayı getiriyor.
Kimi izleyiciler Pattinson'ın seçilmesinden çok memnun. Kimileri ise o kadar değil...
Bu da beklenecek bir durum. Sean Connery rolü aldığında herkes Bond'un Cary Grant olmasını istemişti. Timothy Dalton seçildiğinde, Pierce Brosnan'ın TV yükümlülükleri nedeniyle 007 ceketini giyememesine herkes can sıkmıştı. Daniel Craig açıklandığında ise "fazla kısa", "fazla sıradan", "fazla sarışın"dı. Casino Royale o mızmız eleştirmenlere beton mikseriyle koca bir tevazu pastası yedirdi.
İşte şimdiye kadarki en iyi / en komik / en coşkulu / en alıngan tepkilerden bazıları; üstelik hiçbir kimse değil, doğrudan Kraliyet Ailesi'nin resmi paylaşımıyla başlıyoruz:
"Düşünün, 2008'de birine Twilight'taki Edward'ın James Bond ve Batman olduğunu ve herkesin bundan memnun olduğunu söylediğinizi. Ne tuhaf ama eğlenceli bir kariyeri oldu."
"Twilight resmen Robert Pattinson'ın James Bond olacağını önceden söyledi bu arada."
"Harry Potter. Twilight. Tenet. The Batman. The Odyssey. Primetime. Dune. Ve şimdi JAMES BOND. Cedric Diggory'den Bruce Wayne'e, oradan 007'ye. ROBERT FUCKIN PATTINSON."
"Batman'i VE Bond'u oynamak, İncil'de bahsedilen türden bir açgözlülük; ama rolü Villeneuve'ün yönettiği Pattinson Bond'unda başka kimseyi görmek isteyebileceğimi hayal bile edemiyorum. Villeneuve imzalı Pattinson Bond'u CRACK gibi çarpacak."
"James Bond'un şöyle olması gerekir: Zarif. Sofistike. Son derece zeki. Taş gibi sert. Her erkek onun gibi olmak ister. Her kadın onu ister. Robert Pattinson 007 değil! Berbat bir Batman'di."
"Aptalca karar. Robert Pattinson Bond için uygun malzeme değil. Karşınızda mükemmel adayı bulmuştunuz ve elinizden kaçırdınız. BUNDAN NEFRET EDİYORUM."
"James Bond'un Robert Pattinson tarafından canlandırılmasını sevmeyen tek kişi ben miyim? Hep daha az bilinen bir İngiliz oyuncu için kariyer değiştiren bir şey olmasını sevmiştim."
"Robert Pattinson'ı James Bond olarak seçmek, son derece hayal gücünden yoksun bir karar. Birincisi, Pattinson hâlihazırda Batman. Gerçekten bu kadar oyuncu kıtlığı mı var da her ikonik karakteri aynı birkaç adamın oynaması gerekiyor? İkincisi, beraberinde fazlasıyla bagaj getiriyor. Bond oyuncuları, rol tarafından tanımlanan görece boş sayfalar olmalı; izleyicilerin onlarca yıllık çağrışımlarını beraberinde getiren yerleşik sinema yıldızları değil."
Tüm bu tepkilere rağmen, 2028'de Bond 26 vizyona girene kadar ne olacağını bilemeyeceğiz.
Resmi gösterim tarihi henüz açıklanmadı. Ancak filmi izlediğimizde, ancak o zaman, "Halihazırda Altın Kariyerli Adam"ın Bond'u nasıl kendine özgü kıldığını ve doğru seçim olup olmadığını göreceğiz. Yoksa (Thunder)balls mı olduğunu.

OpenAI lost control of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing, California’s AG claims.
California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face. In a lawsuit filed Monday , Attorney General Rob Bonta accuses OpenAI of violating consumer safety law by knowingly developing a “dangerous product without proper oversight,” as reported earlier by Reuters .
The lawsuit claims the cyberattack on Hugging Face “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability.” It alleges that OpenAI recently told the attorney general’s office that it “lost control” of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing.
After revealing the rogue AI attack on Hugging Face in July, news of several other similar incidents emerged, including attacks on an Australian government website , a German wiki site , and the software package manager RubyGems . OpenAI’s agents also tried to “bruteforce” a United Nations website.
“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-world cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta says in the press release. “The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law.”
OpenAI released its new cybersecurity AI model earlier this month, saying that it’s less likely to go rogue and attack other platforms. It’s also giving safety evaluators at Apollo Research access to its AI systems as part of a pilot program that monitors models for misalignment.
“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says in an emailed statement to The Verge . “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”

OpenAI is facing a new lawsuit from the California Attorney General’s office , alleging that the company’s training practices and lax security pose an ongoing danger to the public.
At the center of the case is the July 2026 Hugging Face compromise , in which a pre-release model within OpenAI compromised both companies’ security systems to complete a training benchmark. In its official report on the incident , OpenAI called it “an outlier scenario involving a rare and unexpected confluence of events.”
The California lawsuit represents one of the first attempts by a government regulator to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident, with significant implications for both OpenAI’s competitors and its clients.
The complaint centers on the Hugging Face incident, but also cites similar incidents involving RubyGems , DseWiki , the Wikimedia Foundation , and Australian government websites as evidence that the underlying behavior is ongoing.
The complaint also alleges that dozens of similar incidents have occurred without public disclosure.
“OpenAI has recently sent notices to dozens of additional third parties whose websites or internal systems have been infiltrated by OpenAI agents,” the complaint reads. “In some cases, OpenAI agents were able to access sensitive personally identifiable information, such as employee records containing names, birth dates, addresses, and more. The vast majority of these incidents have not been disclosed or discussed publicly by either OpenAI or by the affected third parties.”
The central allegation is that OpenAI’s ongoing testing practices constitute a public nuisance because the lack of safety controls present an ongoing risk to the public. A secondary claim alleges unfair competition stemming from the marketing of an unsafe product. If the lawsuit succeeds, OpenAI could face an injunction “to abate the ongoing public nuisance,” leaving broad discretion in the hands of the court.
It’s the first regulatory case targeting OpenAI specifically over rogue agent incidents, although public endangerment claims have been considered by other states. In June, the Florida attorney general sued the company over allegedly harmful effects on users , particularly children and teenagers. In August, the Alabama attorney general launched a probe into deceptive practices related to the breach, but no case has been filed.
In a statement to the press, California Attorney General Rob Bonta presented the case as an effort to maintain public safety in the face of a powerful new technology.
“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society. The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it,” Bonta said in the statement. “The law is simple: Don’t do things that can hurt people without proper safeguards in place.”

The lawsuit stems from an earlier incident where the tech company’s products hacked into the open-source platform Hugging Face
California sued OpenAI on Monday, accusing the artificial intelligence titan of developing its technology without safety or the public’s interest in mind.
The lawsuit concerns an incident earlier this year where OpenAI agents – semi-autonomous AI software that can carry out digital actions on behalf of users – launched a cyber-attack into the open-source AI platform Hugging Face.
Rob Bonta, California’s attorney general, said the “infamous” attack was just one of 80 known incidents involving “loss of control” and shows that OpenAI doesn’t have adequate safeguards in place to protect society.
“While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability,” Bonta said in a statement.
The lawsuit, filed in state superior court in San Francisco, alleges OpenAI violated California’s Unfair Competition Law and is a public nuisance as defined by state law. Bonta is asking the court to order OpenAI to change its business practices and pay civil penalties.
California’s lawsuit follows Bonta’s formal investigation into OpenAI, launched in September, over the Hugging Face incident, followed by a subpoena of the company probing other cybersecurity incidents and risks with its models. The Federal Trade Commission is also conducting an industry-wide investigation into OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI labs over the potential dangers their technology poses to consumers’ digital security.
In July, OpenAI revealed that one of its autonomous AI agents went rogue during a test , accessing the open web and hacking into Hugging Face. The company called it an “unprecedented cyber-incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities”.
Since then, several other incidents involving OpenAI have come to light, including a breach of government websites in Australia. Other AI firms, including Anthropic and Google, have also disclosed rogue agent activity .
Drew Pusateri, a spokesperson for OpenAI, said the company has worked to create safeguards for its AI models, along with identifying and disclosing incidents of “misalignment”. He said most cases identified have been low severity with limited-to-no impact.
“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” Pusateri said. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab.”
During a press conference, Bonta said OpenAI violated the law and that his suit is meant to ensure the company puts proper safeguards in place. He noted that the possibility exists for AI agents to hack into the power grid and medical and financial institutions.
“These risks are no longer hypothetical,” Bonta said. “Without sufficient safeguards and controls, the scope and frequency of this already unacceptable risk will only increase.”

California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the ChatGPT-maker misled and endangered the public by developing artificial intelligence (AI) models without proper safeguards.
In the lawsuit, Bonta cited the July 2026 attack on the AI platform Hugging Face by experimental OpenAI agents which accessed the internet to breach that company's internal systems.
Bonta claimed OpenAI created a public nuisance and violated the state's unfair competition laws.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the BBC in a statement that Bonta's lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab".
Other major AI developers including Anthropic, Meta, and Google have also said their models have staged similar attacks.
But Bonta's lawsuit, filed in San Francisco, where the company is headquartered, appears to be the first such suit filed by a US state.
Warning shot or publicity stunt - how worried should we be about the OpenAI hack?
Hundreds of OpenAI agents coordinated the Hugging Face attack over two days even though they were supposed to be contained in a safe testing environment.
The incident drew added scrutiny because the agents went as far as attempting to cover their tracks.
Bonta announced an investigation into the incident in September, and served an investigative subpoena on OpenAI as part of its probe.
"The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it - this disregard for public safety violated California law," Bonta said in a statement on Monday.
OpenAI said it has been transparent and responsive to the Attorney General's office.
"We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged - and will continue to engage - constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry," the company said.
The company added that, since the Hugging Face incident, it has worked to understand and address "misaligned model activity" which industry figures often refer to as rogue agents.
Nathan Calvin, chief strategy officer at AI safety campaign group Encode AI, said the lawsuit "recognises something we at Encode have long raised alarms about".
"OpenAI and other companies developing frontier AI systems have safety and security practices that are insufficient to protect the public from risks that could be catastrophic," he said.

Airline acknowledges ‘technology issue that delayed flight departures’ in latest high-profile outage to affect Americans
United ⁠Airlines said on ⁠Monday ⁠that it had resolved ⁠a widespread system ⁠outage, just three days after the Federal ⁠Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop on all US flights.
“We have resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures. While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,” Chicago-based United said in a statement. “There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.”
According to an internal memo from ​United’s pilots’ ‌union seen ‌by Reuters, a company-wide ‌web-based outage had affected multiple applications used by pilots, including crew communications. It said United was unable to provide final ‌aircraft weights for departing flights and advised pilots to ​follow airport station guidance on whether to leave their gates.
Before every departure, pilots use performance software, often on a cockpit tablet, to check that the aircraft can safely take off under current weather and runway conditions. The preflight calculations include the aircraft’s weight along with information about the fuel, baggage, cargo and passengers the plane is carrying.
Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said in an interview Monday night that he did not know what caused the one-and-a-half-hour outage. “This is not ‌an FAA [Federal Aviation Administration] system-wide problem,” Duffy said on Hannity on Fox News.
The United computer issue is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown to affect Americans in the last few days. On Friday, ageing equipment led to a temporary grounding of all commercial airplanes in the US for more than four hours, sparking travel chaos as thousands of flights were delayed or canceled.
Airlines have experienced similar disruptions before. ‌In August 2025, United temporarily grounded flights after a problem with its Unimatic system, which supplies flight information to systems used to calculate aircraft weight and balance. It was not immediately clear whether Monday’s outage ​involved United’s Unimatic system.
The Trump administration said the rare ground stop stemmed from a fiber upgrade during routine maintenance that led to data flooding, which crashed a critical communication system.
And earlier on Monday, customers reported service outages and difficulty accessing their online accounts at several major US banks and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.
It also comes after a major outage by Microsoft that began on Thursday and lasted into the next day, which crippled a host of services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot. The outage had serious repercussions for millions of people and organizations all over the world, including schools, hospitals, businesses, courts, banks, prisons, police forces and governments.
Microsoft said it had resolved the issue and restored service by Saturday, also issuing an apology. The office software giant did not attribute the blackout to a cybersecurity breach, identifying in an initial report on Monday that a combination of a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections, and server capacity sparked the outage.

Amazon MGM Studios'un yeni James Bond filmi için bekleyiş sürüyor. Aylar süren oyuncu seçmeleri ve tartışmalar sonucu Yeni James Bond belli oldu.
"007" karakterini oynayacak olan ismin İngiliz oyuncu Robert Pattinson olduğu açıklandı.
Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan ve Daniel Craig'den sonra James Bond rolünü üstlenecek yedinci oyuncu olan Pattinson, heyecanını şu sözlerle paylaştı:
“007 rolünün bana emanet edilmesi hayatımın en büyük onuru. Bana güvendikleri için Denis, Amy, David, Tanya ve Amazon MGM Studios'taki herkese minnettarım. Bu rolün bir hayalin gerçekleşmesi olduğunu söylemek bile yaşadığım heyecanı anlatmaya yetmez. Bu işbirliğinden ve böylesine harika bir ekiple çalışacak olmaktan dolayı büyük heyecan duyuyorum.”
Yeni James Bond filminin 2028 yılında vizyona girmesi bekleniyor.
James Bond 'u oynayacak ismin açıklanması sonrası gözler serinin vazgeçilmezi Bond kızına çevrildi. Yeni “007” filminde ikonik Bond kızı rolünün kime emanet edileceği merak konusu olurken, bazı isimler öne çıktı. İşte Bond kızı olabilecek yıldızlar…

Son dönemin yükselen yıldızları arasında yer alan Florence Pugh, daha önce canlandırdığı Black Widow karakteri sebebiyle dövüş sahnelerindeki deneyimiyle öne çıkıyor. 30 yaşındaki oyuncu, aynı zamanda Dune 3'te de Pattinson'la rol aldı.

Watch: As new Bond, Pattinson takes on one of film's most high-profile roles
Robert Pattinson, the British actor known for films such as Twilight and The Batman, has been confirmed as the next actor to play James Bond.
The announcement was made by Amazon MGM Studios in a social media post on Monday, with a picture showing Pattinson in character as 007.
The 40-year-old becomes the seventh actor to play the famous fictional spy and will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028.
In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime."
The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve and written by Steven Knight, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.
In his statement, Pattinson said he was "deeply grateful" to the film's creative team "for their belief in me".
"To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement," he added. "I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."
The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Daniel Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment.
The next 007 film will be the first since long-term Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson stepped back and Amazon took creative control of the franchise, after acquiring the series' parent company MGM.
By the time the 26th Bond film is released, it will have been seven years since the last - 2021's No Time To Die - the biggest gap in the franchise's history.
'Big shoes to fill': Robert Pattinson asked about playing Bond in 2010
Director Villeneuve is best known for films including the Dune trilogy, Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival and Blade Runner 2049, while writer Knight is known for TV hits Peaky Blinders and House of Guinness, and films including Burnt, Spencer and Locke.
Pattinson has already worked with Villeneuve on Dune: Part 3, where he stars as a new villain, Scytale. The film is released next month.
In a statement reacting to Pattinson's Bond casting, Villeneuve said: "Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey.
"We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond.
"He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin."
Robert Pattinson has starred in Twilight, Tenet, The Batman and The Odyssey
Pattinson's casting was also welcomed by Buckingham Palace, with a post on Instagram sharing the news and adding: "Welcome to His Majesty's Secret Service, Mr Bond."
Australian actor George Lazenby, who played James Bond in the 1969 film On Her Majesty's Secret, posted a video on social media welcoming Pattinson to "the most exclusive club in the world".
"Remember to enjoy yourself... Let's see if you'll have 'this never happened to the other fella' moment," Lazenby said.
Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks.
But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands.
Producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman said the "legacy of James Bond is in great hands with Robert Pattinson".
"His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times."
At 40, Pattinson is one of the older actors who was thought to have auditioned for the role of Bond.
Reports last week suggested Pattinson's deal committed him to playing 007 for three films, , external rather than the four that had reportedly been discussed with some of the other actors, but that has not been officially confirmed.
Pattinson shot to fame in Harry Potter and went on to star in Twilight opposite Kristen Stewart (pictured in 2011)
Robert Pattinson shot to fame as Cedric Diggory in 2005's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire.
He went on to play vampire Edward Cullen in Twilight, the hugely popular film series based on Stephenie Meyer's best-selling novels.
Pattinson starred opposite Kristen Stewart in five Twilight films in total, which collectively made more than $3bn (£2.2bn) at the box office worldwide.
He has gone on to star in other major films such as 2022's The Batman and Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, released earlier this year.
But he is also respected within the industry for how many roles he has taken in smaller movies - often independent, experimental or arthouse films.
His other credits include The Lighthouse, Mickey 17, Life, The Drama, Good Time, The Rover, Bel Ami, Primetime, Tenet and The Lost City of Z.
Pattinson follows in the footsteps of only six actors to have played James Bond in the official film series – Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig.
Daniel Craig was a popular 007 and appeared in five James Bond films
Craig appeared in five Bond movies in total, starting with 2006's Casino Royale, and spent 16 years as the secret agent created by author Ian Fleming.
In a statement, Fleming's estate said they were "delighted to welcome Robert Pattinson to the James Bond family".
The next film will mark a new era for the franchise. Amazon purchased MGM for $8.5bn in 2021, which included the rights to distribute James Bond.
Then in 2025, long-time Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson agreed to sell creative control of the franchise to Amazon MGM.
Before that, the franchise had been under the Broccoli family's control since 1962's Dr. No, when Sean Connery first starred as Bond.
The Broccoli family preserved the integrity of the character and brand for decades, resisting spin-offs and licensing that some industry experts now expect to see following Amazon's takeover.

The latest numbers are in on how much energy hyperscale data centers use and the carbon pollution they create.
Fossil fuels are still the biggest source of electricity for hyperscale data centers in the US, a new paper published in the journal Nature Sustainability shows. They likely burn through more electricity collectively than many countries do, resulting in a serious amount of greenhouse gas emissions.
The study homes in on hyperscale facilities — the massive structures spanning millions of square feet that developers are racing to build in large part to support generative AI. Researchers say the findings show that there’s a lot of work left to do to cut down pollution stemming from AI’s reliance on fossil fuels.
“We tend to discuss AI’s environmental footprint as though it were some fixed property of the technology, when in reality the same computing infrastructure can have dramatically different consequences depending on the electricity system supporting it,” Gianluca Guidi, lead author of the new study and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, says in an email to The Verge. “I actually find that encouraging, because it means these impacts aren’t inevitable. We have choices about where we build and how we power this infrastructure.”
“The same computing infrastructure can have dramatically different consequences depending on the electricity system supporting it.”
Guidi and his team used satellite imagery to identify 403 hyperscale data centers in the US, estimating each facility’s power consumption based on its electrical capacity. Using data from the Environmental Protection Agency, they approximated how much carbon pollution each data center would have produced if connected to the local power grid between May 2024 and April 2025.
Altogether, the 403 hyperscale facilities likely consumed around 82 terawatt-hours of electricity that year, about 1.8 percent of all US electricity consumption. That’s even more than the amount of electricity that about 148 nations — a majority of the countries in the world including Austria, Israel, and Venezuela but excluding the largest economies including the US and China — individually burn through each year, according to John Sterman, director of the MIT System Dynamics group and MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative.
Electricity demand from these data centers produced 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 emissions, comparable to the annual carbon footprint of Denmark, according to the research paper. Sterman says that exceeds the total carbon emissions of about 113 nations. That’s because about 54 percent of the electricity the hyperscale facilities consumed likely came from gas and coal.
Sterman, who was not involved in the research with Guidi, disclosed that he used the help of Claude to compare the paper’s findings to electricity use and emissions of countries. “I think AI can be extraordinarily helpful,” Sterman says. “But we’ve got to figure out a way to limit the harms … Especially because those impacts are irreversible. Once you allow these data centers to emit the CO2, you can never undo that.”
Sterman says policymakers should require data center operators to bring new clean energy online. The study doesn’t account for local air pollution that can result from new gas infrastructure that’s being built to meet data center demand, or gas turbines that some AI companies have installed at their facilities to power themselves without connecting to the grid. And while hyperscale data centers encompass more than just AI-related computing, they also make up just a fraction of the thousands of data centers in the US — with more cropping up each year.
The study showed how big a difference the local electricity mix makes when it comes to the environmental impact of AI and data centers. Generating electricity in heavily coal-reliant Wyoming led to roughly seven times more carbon emissions per kilowatt-hour than in hydropower-rich Oregon. “Two data centers consuming exactly the same amount of electricity can have dramatically different carbon footprints simply because of where they’re located,” Guidi writes.
Fengqi You, a professor in energy systems engineering at Cornell University who was also not involved in the study, says the results highlight the problem of “long-term carbon lock-in.” “Power plants and supporting infrastructure built to meet rapidly growing data center demand may operate for decades. Decisions made today could therefore shape emissions well into the future,” You says in an email to The Verge.
Both You and Guidi also pointed out how problematic it is that researchers have to go through such great lengths to estimate energy consumption because data center operators won’t disclose that information. To that end, Guidi and his colleagues are using their research to build a website to track the environmental impact of individual data centers. A bipartisan bill making its way through Congress could also mandate greater disclosures nationally on data centers’ electricity use.
“Communities and policymakers need reliable, independent data on what these facilities mean for our air, health, and the climate. This study is an important step.” Gina McCarthy, former White House national climate advisor and EPA administrator, said in a statement shared by the research authors.

Trump administration introduces export licence requirements for Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Singapore and Brazil.
United States President Donald Trump’s administration has announced new restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips amid fallout from the alleged spy scandal involving AI giant Nvidia.
The rule announced by the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) on Monday aims to prevent Chinese AI developers from getting around export controls by remotely accessing data centres in third countries, particularly in Southeast Asia.
It designates Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil as countries with an “unacceptable risk of diversion” and requires anyone seeking to ship advanced chips to those destinations to obtain an export licence.
BIS, which sits under the Department of Commerce, said the change was a “logical extension” of the existing requirement for companies to obtain a licence to export or transfer chips to firms based in China.
“The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten US national security,” BIS said in a statement.
While Chinese firms are barred from importing the most advanced graphics processing units (GPUs) under US export controls, they had until now been legally able to take advantage of remote access to top-of-the-line computing power at data centres in countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.
Singapore, which hosts dozens of data centres, said on Tuesday that it was “studying the details of this new measure carefully”.
“We are engaging affected companies to understand the potential impact on their businesses,” the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry and the Ministry of Digital Development and Information said in a joint statement.
“We have also been engaging the relevant US authorities on the scope and implementation of the measure, as well as exploring how to facilitate trusted access for Singapore companies.”
The ministries added that they did not condone companies using Singapore to “circumvent or violate” the laws of other countries.
The restrictions come as Nvidia’s export of advanced chips is under scrutiny following claims that former CEO Jensen Huang was romantically involved with a woman recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security for espionage.
Huang, who became one of the most prominent faces of the AI boom at the helm of Nvidia, resigned last week amid a company board investigation into allegations involving the Chinese-born executive of Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.
Beijing has denied the spying allegations, made by unnamed US officials in media reports, calling them “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.
Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive identified as Jensen Huang’s ex-romantic partner, has not publicly commented on the claims.
Late on Monday, the US Commerce Department and the Department of Justice publicly confirmed that investigators had opened a criminal investigation into Megaspeed.
The Commerce Department began investigating Megaspeed for potential export control violations in 2024, leading BIS officials to conduct an on-site inspection of the Singapore-based company and to interview Alice Huang the following year, the statement said.
The Justice Department subsequently took the “lead role” in the criminal investigation, according to the statement.
“The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” it said.
US tech stocks fell sharply on Monday as investors weighed the scandal’s fallout on the AI rollout.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 2.5 percent, closing in the red for the third consecutive session.
Shares of Nvidia, which have shed more than 30 percent of their market value over the past month, dropped 4.1 percent.
The other six companies of the “Magnificent Seven” also lost ground, with Alphabet and Amazon seeing the next-biggest declines of 4.1 percent and 3.3 percent, respectively.
The sell-off continued in Asia on Tuesday, with key indexes in Japan, South Korea and Hong Kong closing in the red.
Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 and South Korea’s Kospi closed down 1.3 percent and 2.6 percent, respectively, while the Hang Seng Index in Hong Kong dropped 0.9 percent.

Producers cite “his fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit” and continual reinvention as factors.
The Internet has been abuzz for months about which actor would replace Daniel Craig as British agent 007 James Bond in the franchise. We finally have the answer: Robert Pattinson , who built on his 2005 role as the doomed Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire into an illustrious career mixing roles in franchises and Hollywood blockbusters with daring arthouse fare.
“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement . “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”
The choice will reunite Pattinson with Denis Villeneuve, who recently worked with him on the forthcoming Dune: Part III and will direct the next (as yet untitled) Bond installment. “I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey,” Villeneuve said in a statement . We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.”
Not everyone is happy with the casting choice ; some have never forgiven Pattinson for the Twilight franchise, despite the actor’s impressive recent films. Pattinson has played darker roles in recent years, often as a villain. And at 40, Pattinson is a bit older than the actors he beat out, most notably Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden ( Slow Horses ), Josh O’Connor ( Wake Up, Dead Man ), and Callum Turner ( Fantastic Beasts ).
But Pattinson is a logical choice for Bond; heck, he’s already played a secret agent in Christopher Nolan’s Tenet (2020). In fact, he originally topped the list of longtime Bond franchise steward Barbara Broccoli’s and Michael G. Wilson’s choices to take over from Craig. They shelved that idea when Pattinson was cast in Matt Reeves’ The Batman . But Broccoli and Wilson no longer have creative control over Bond, having sold the rights to Amazon MGM for $20 million.
Pattinson’s box office record this year probably didn’t hurt either: He played central roles in The Drama , Primetime , and The Odyssey , all of which made back their production costs and then some, with Dune: Part III still to come. It’s unclear how his Bond commitments will affect Pattinson’s future as Batman; The Batman: Part 2 has faced production delays (and a director change) and is slated for a 2028 release. Should there be a third installment—not assured in the wake of James Gunn and Peter Safran’s departure from DC Studios —Reeves will likely work around Pattinson’s Bond schedule.
“James Bond is one of the most beloved, inspiring, iconic and yet enigmatic characters in literature and movies,” producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman said in a statement . “The legacy of this character is in great hands with Robert Pattinson. His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times.”

Trump bets China won’t mind US blocking remote access to AI chips.
On the heels of the Nvidia scandal , the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training.
In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department said it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.
US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said. Among threats, the US fears rivals could use advanced AI to develop “more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.”
Now, the rules have been tightened up so much that the South China Morning Post reported that, “as a result, any advanced chips made for a Chinese firm are assumed to be restricted, and factories must ask the US government for a license before shipping them.”
The rule change takes effect 90 days after it’s posted to the Federal Register. Moving forward, companies headquartered in any of those countries deemed to “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to China, Russia, and Iran must apply for a license with strict know-your-customer controls when transferring high volumes of advanced chips. If a license is granted, companies will have to “perform robust due diligence,” submitting monthly reports on transactions that thoroughly detail all parties involved, as well as their parent companies, and the final destination for chips sold.
In a press release Sunday, the Commerce Department described the rule change as “designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.” An exception was carved out for companies providing computing power “exclusively used for commercial recommender systems.” The Department said it was acting to “prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.”
Without the intervention, officials fear that China could develop a military or economic edge, The New York Times reported .
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman, Alice Huang, suspected of serving as a Chinese spy . Congress is probing if Alice Huang used her personal relationship with Jensen Huang to help her former company, Megaspeed, become one of Nvidia’s biggest customers, then used that position to smuggle Nvidia’s restricted AI chips into China. China has denied that Alice Huang was a spy, and Megaspeed has denied that smuggling occurred, while launching its own internal probe.
Megaspeed is a Singaporean data center firm whose primary business is cloud computing and AI infrastructure. Prior to the rule change, selling remote access to AI servers to customers in China was perfectly legal, NYT noted. But now, the Commerce Department has given firms like Megaspeed 90 days to either obtain licenses or face future export restrictions.
Whether or not to add more chip curbs has been a polarizing debate in the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly butted heads with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. When the Megaspeed news broke, Bessent pushed for curbs, but Lutnick reportedly appeared “too cozy” with Nvidia to move. Instead, Lutnick initially favored looser controls that Nvidia claimed would ensure global dominance of US technology. (A Commerce Department spokesperson told NYT that Bessent has never confronted Lutnick over his handling of Megaspeed.)
Any companies found violating the rules could face a “range of consequences,” the Commerce Department said after reportedly bending to Bessent’s pressure campaign. Those include possibly facing new import restrictions, stricter license requirements, downgrading their status in the US export control regime, or other changes to their company’s or their base country’s entity-list designations.
Although the summary of the rule change said that “Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion” of the anti-diversion policy, it’s unclear how aggressively the Commerce Department might enforce the rule, NYT noted.
Bessent has publicly criticized Lutnick for failing to sanction Megaspeed, and NYT reported that ultimately, enforcement of the stricter rules—which Bessent helped draft—“would be up to the Commerce Department.”
“The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?” Bessent said on a CNBC appearance. “I think it’s important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that.”
There’s even a push to oust Lutnick over his position on chips, but The Guardian reported that Donald Trump confirmed he has no plans to replace the AI industry-friendly commerce secretary. On Monday, Trump told reporters that Lutnick was right to delay blacklisting Megaspeed, because “if you didn’t delay it… you could have a blow-up with China.”
At the press gaggle, Trump aligned with China in saying that there’s no evidence yet that Alice Huang was a spy. He also joined a band of prominent tech leaders calling for Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, saying that it wasn’t a “bad idea.”
“Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy,” Trump said. “She may not be a spy.”
However, US investigators have alleged that they found “Alice Huang used industry contacts and a series of shell companies to access 240,000 chips banned for export into China,” CBS News reported .
China is unlikely to welcome the new rules, as it has consistently accused the US of fabricating the spying claims to justify imposing additional chip restrictions.
However, a senior Trump official, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive policy matters, told the NYT that Trump “did not expect countermeasures from China in response.”
Trump will be in China for an economic summit this week, including a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The new curbs could potentially disrupt those talks, according to Hong Yuan, a researcher and secretary-general of the Center for American Military Studies at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. Hong told the People’s Daily that China will likely view the rule change as politically motivated.
“Before any judicial causality was established, Washington handed down a political conviction, substituting suspicion for proof, espionage for personal contact, and an industrial embargo for private conduct,” Hong said. “The issue is not the cause of tighter controls, but a political catalyst.”
The new policy could hurt the US, experts told the Chinese outlets. Analysts told the South China Morning Post that the policy could “accelerate Chinese companies’ shift to domestic AI chips.” Other experts told the People’s Daily—which is the official newspaper of the Chinese Communist Party—that “the cost of switching back to US platforms will rise” over time. If that happened, it could potentially lock in Chinese technology over America’s in “the world’s largest single consumer market for chips,” experts said.

Study attempts to tally hyperscalers’ energy use and emissions.
One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built.
A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference to track moving forward.
The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts.
In a way, that makes this a very conservative estimate, since 272 facilities believed to be large data centers were left out. But if you’re interested in AI data centers, specifically, it’s also true that some of the facilities included may not fall in that category.
That fact also introduces some uncertainty in the actual power usage of these data centers. Relying on other research, they use a range—some conventional data centers run at an average of about 48 percent of capacity, while AI training loads have been running higher, at around 70 percent.
Putting that together, the total power usage for the year by these 403 data centers was estimated at 68 to 99 terawatt-hours. That amounts to 1.5 to 2.2 percent of total US electricity use, on par with the total used by Wisconsin or Indiana.
A recent Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report estimated the total electricity use of all data centers of any kind in the US (minus crypto mining) at 76 terawatt-hours in 2018. In 2024, that number was up to 192 terawatt-hours. That means the hyperscale data centers identified by this study account for something like one-third to one-half of all data center energy use.
The researchers also wanted to estimate the greenhouse gas emissions associated with generating all that electricity. It’s fairly straightforward to get a reasonable number here—calculate the mix of generation in each data center’s region of the grid, and apply that CO 2 per watt-hour rate to a data center’s electricity use.
This yields 21 to 31 million metric tons of CO 2 for the year. That’s around 0.5 percent of total US fossil fuel CO 2 emissions.
These data centers aren’t located in areas of especially clean energy—their energy mix was only slightly cleaner than the US average. About 54 percent of the electricity was generated by fossil fuel power plants (dominantly natural gas), with 25 percent from renewables, and 21 percent from nuclear.
This doesn’t include any “behind-the-meter” generation on-site, though. The xAI data center in Tennessee notably ran a fleet of natural gas turbines during this study’s time period, for example. Cleanview, which describes itself as a market intelligence company, has tracked a boom in on-site generation since early 2025, including 116 current or planned data centers. While this may not affect this study’s numbers much, it is becoming increasingly significant over time.
This matters because the types of generators being used are much less efficient than utility power plants, emitting 60 to 80 percent more greenhouse gases to produce the same amount of electricity. (Conversely, if a data center built solar generation instead, it could reduce the carbon footprint of its energy.)
Although this study can’t pinpoint the energy use of AI data centers alone, repeating this analysis in subsequent years could reveal the growth related to the AI buildout—at least as long as that buildout lasts.
Nature Sustainability, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41893-026-01985-7 ( About DOIs ).

You’d think that Oobah Butler would have run out of schemes by now.
The gonzo British documentarian’s repertoire includes creating an entirely fake restaurant —The Shed at Dulwich—and getting it to the top spot on London’s Tripadvisor; selling bottles of Amazon drivers’ urine on the ecommerce site; and convincing venture capitalists to give him $1 million .
But as his new HBO show, Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow , makes perfectly clear, Butler still has plenty of tricks up his sleeve—and it’s a delight to watch them unfold.
The series launches November 22. Each of the premier season’s five episodes centers on Butler scamming his way into success in a different industry—wellness, wine, dating, music, and a finale I do not want to spoil—with increasingly outlandish ideas that, somehow, almost no one advises him against.
His shock of bleach-blond hair and appearance of a Victorian ghost notwithstanding, there are undeniable similarities between Butler’s style and that of master of manipulation Nathan Fielder . Both use satire and parody to make social commentaries, and both often divert from their original plans by hyperfocusing on what the average person might consider a tangential detail, carrying these side quests to extreme lengths. But while Fielder has sometimes been criticized for roping unassuming working-class folks into his hijinks, in Butler’s case the joke is almost always on the rich and powerful—and the systems that allow them to prevail.
“The whole show can be reduced to ‘monkey see, monkey do,’” Butler tells me from a coffee shop at the New York Historical Society in Manhattan, where he’s just ordered a latte with four espresso shots and been recognized from TikTok by a fellow patron. “I just find these bad actors and copy them.”
Butler’s knack for convincing high-profile—in some cases notorious—executives and tastemakers to appear on camera and earnestly weigh in on his ridiculous plans at times boggles the mind. In the series premiere, he sets out to start a wellness company that sells the tears of human children as a skin serum, and gets none other than former Theranos chief creative officer Patrick O’Neill to consult on a marketing strategy.
Applying his characteristic charm, Butler tells O’Neill he “smashed it” with creating mystique around the scandal-plagued biotech startup, to which O’Neill replies, “Thank you, yeah. I think it’s good to share the knowledge.”
Butler wearing glasses designed to collect the tears of children.
After briefly expressing hesitancy around the ethical sourcing of the tears, O’Neill begins offering Butler packaging advice: a tear-shaped bottle, and the two discuss the name Lacrimé (“tears” in Italian). “It makes it feel exotic and not necessarily something you’d see from Johnson and Johnson,” O’Neill says, in all seriousness.
Confiding in $1,500-an-hour lawyer Jennifer Keller about how he may have committed fraud with his wellness venture, Butler tells her the industry is “a gold rush of bullshit. And I want in.” She laughs and says that he sounds “more and more like an American.” It’s all very funny, but as the name of the show hints, there is a Robin Hood quality to Butler’s scamming, in this case exposing the poorly regulated nature of skin care and supplements.
Butler has chosen the New York Historical Society as our meeting point because he loves history, and New York’s in particular. When he first moved here in February 2024, he started reading Robert Caro’s The Power Broker , a biography of influential urban planner Robert Moses, giving him an understanding of “how power works” in the city. But his itch to move came well before that, when he visited in 2016.
“I just found it so inspiring,” he says, dressed in a maroon velvet shirt, baggy dark jeans, and Salomon sneakers, a Patagonia backpack slung over his shoulders, as we set out for a walk in Central Park. “I got to an age where I just thought, well if I don’t do this now, I probably am not going to do it.”
Although New York is indeed full of power brokers—and very wealthy ones at that—he says it’s different from the aristocracy he grew up around in Feckenham, a 700-person “Hobbiton-style village” in the UK.
“I grew up in a lower-class family … I’ve definitely got a bit of a chip on my shoulder about class,” he says, noting that he’s the youngest of six siblings. “And America, for all of its issues, there is something amazing about how I see the same guys who really wind me up in the UK—upper-class kind of guys—and the way that they walk the earth and the way they feel and the way they carry themselves. I see them come here and no one gives a shit. Really, truly, no one gives a shit.”
Butler didn't go to college. He started a band called My Grey Horse in 2010, playing guitar and singing. Around the age of 17, he began writing music reviews, secretly hoping to score his band some coverage. “It was a scam on the go,” he says. But he caught the writing bug, finding it “meditative.” Later, he joined VICE (where I previously worked as a senior reporter) as a freelance video host, making a bunch of documentaries, including the extremely viral one about The Shed. From there, he did several films for the UK’s Channel 4 and cohosted MTV’s Catfish UK .
“It changed my life and was absolutely the right thing to do. I wouldn't have been able to afford to move here if I hadn't done Catfish ,” he says.
Though he tells me he’s not a comedian, Butler is a natural clown, and at times even just his buffoonish mannerisms are enough to elicit laughs. Maybe he’s such a natural because he comes from a long line of schemers. He tells me his great grandfather moved to the US in the late 19th century as part of the fur trade, but he would also sell rabbit droppings rolled in flour as medicine.
Though he may not have firsthand experiences, Butler’s perceptions of hoity-toity cultural institutions—and their vulnerabilities—are spot on. In an episode about fine wine, he embarks on a mission to sell a smoke-tainted swill brand called Fumare as a high-end product—even though it would normally be tossed by wine producers or used for barbecue sauces. Part of his task is to convince New York Times wine critic Eric Asimov to give the smoked wine a good review.
Butler creates a psychological profile of Asimov, determining that he’s a “contrarian” who “wants to be romanced.” Knowing he’s a fan of Bob Dylan, Butler just happens to be playing a Dylan song on the piano when Asimov shows up for a tasting. While Asimov pans the first glass of smoky wine, Butler tries again, by pretending it's actually a glass of Barolo, the same stuff Asimov says he fell in love with when he first got into wine. “I have no complaints,” Asimov says—an endorsement that Butler promptly attaches to Fumare’s label.
In another episode, Butler starts an AI dating company called Sole, but instead of matching people with a chatbot, as he’s purporting to do, he matches them with other humans to see if they connect.
“The idea was that people trust in the technology more than a conversation with one another,” he says.
These days, many of Butler’s stunts either directly or indirectly relate to Big Tech—for good reason.
“A lot of it is built on speculative promises and the idea of utopia rather than connected to reality. Tech CEOs constantly coming out and lying about what they’ll be able to do in 10 years to shit-coin their stock price,” he says, adding that the sector is “riddled with inauthenticity.”
Despite having the backing of HBO, his own work still feels authentic and haphazard, as opposed to overly polished. He says it’s usually just him and a couple of other people carrying out the stunts. “One of the episodes was basically me and me in my bedroom,” he says, noting that while he’s been working on the finale for six years, originally envisioning it as a feature film, all the others except for the pilot were shot in the last eight months.

AI systems can allow militaries to find and annihilate targets within seconds. A meaningful treaty must prioritise human control – and accountability
M ilitaries around the world are increasingly relying on artificial intelligence to find, track and annihilate targets. An upcoming conference in Geneva offers a chance to confront the gravest risks of AI-enabled warfare, ideally through a treaty to regulate autonomous weapons systems.
A strike that might have taken half an hour and required significant human consideration only a few years ago can now take minutes, or even seconds, with AI systems taking the lead if they meet a confidence threshold set by a human operator.
In Iran, the US relied on AI-enabled targeting to strike 1,000 targets in the first 24 hours of its attacks in February, during which a school in Minab was bombed , killing more than 120 children. The Russia-Ukraine war has seen extensive use of AI-enabled drones with little or no human input in the final stages of a strike.
Across the Middle East, the Israel Defense Forces have used their “Lavender”, “The Gospel” and “Where’s Daddy?” systems to identify alleged militants and their homes as potential bombing targets. Lavender assisted in the targeting of 37,000 Palestinians in Gaza in the months following 7 October 2023, bypassing what a senior Israeli commander chillingly described as a “human bottleneck for both locating the new targets and decision-making to approve the targets”.
These instances are not now outliers, but rather indicate a wider global trend. This now requires a commensurate global policy and legal response to ensure that human beings and states are held accountable for military decisions – not machines or AI systems.
It can seem daunting, if not impossible, to challenge superpowers’ military doctrines and impose tough regulation on weapons systems. But I know from personal experience that it can be done.
Nearly 40 years ago, I played a role in the passage of the legislation which declared New Zealand to be a nuclear-free state . The New Zealand Nuclear Free Zone, Disarmament, and Arms Control Act 1987 to this day bans the entry of all nuclear weapons and nuclear-powered vessels to New Zealand, and has enjoyed a consistently high level of public support since it was first introduced.
Today, we need a comparable level of global ambition in the face of morally and legally complex new challenges.
When an autonomous weapons system assists in committing a war crime, accountability becomes difficult to establish. The risks are particularly acute for anti-personnel weapons – which are designed to target and strike people, rather than vehicles or buildings. These weapons struggle to distinguish between combatant, journalist, civilian or child.
As Pope Leo XIV stated in his recent encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas : “Any technology that facilitates attacks without seeing the face of human beings lowers the moral threshold of conflict”.
Despite these clear and growing concerns, those governments with the most advanced autonomous weapons systems have long resisted binding limits on their development and use. While they have dragged their feet, the technology, data-processing systems and related surveillance tools have continued to advance at breakneck speed. The gap between technological capability and regulatory constraint is widening day by day.
Given that some of these technologies are cheap to produce and easy to copy, there is a significant risk that non-state actors, including terrorist groups, could obtain them. It is in all states’ interests to avoid such a catastrophic outcome.
When states meet this week at the seventh review conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons in Geneva, they face a choice between launching negotiations on treaty provisions covering these weapons, or allowing more autonomous weapons on to our battlefields and beyond.
Simply agreeing to negotiate a treaty would be a positive outcome given the fractious state of international relations today. With the right level of political will and ambition, these talks can lead to genuinely transformative outcomes, as we have seen in previous decades with binding agreements to ban the use of chemical weapons and anti-personnel landmines.
A meaningful treaty would prioritise human control, accountability and non-proliferation. It would ban autonomous weapons systems which cannot comply with international humanitarian law. All other autonomous weapons would be regulated, including through limited engagement and targeting, human supervision and testing and evaluation.
Those countries which benefit most from the existing lack of accountability may seek to thwart efforts to negotiate a meaningful treaty. That makes it all the more important that the majority of states act collectively to create a safer future, through perseverance, cooperation and courage. A weak treaty which placates those resisting accountability cannot do that.
Technology will not stand still while diplomats struggle to reach consensus; if states do not seize the moment now, our future collective security risks being ever more endangered.
Helen Clark is former head of the UN Development Programme and former prime minister of New Zealand, and member of The Elders
