New tech wealth, amassed with remarkable speed, is now washing up on British shores
S porting hoodies and white trainers rather than the gilets of London’s banker and lawyer class, tech bros can struggle to be taken seriously by the capital’s luxury property agents. “We worked with a young tech entrepreneur with a substantial budget, who agents assumed was looking to rent a one-bedroom flat,” says Jo Eccles, a buying agent who sources off-market properties for ultra-wealthy clients.
But this week’s float by Anthropic, the AI developer behind the chatbot Claude, promises to bring even more credibility for the growing cohort of tech millionaires, which could breathe life into London’s ailing high-end property market . Its IPO on Thursday, expected to value the company at $1.4tn (£1.1tn), is likely to turn more than 4,000 of its staff into millionaires as their stock options vest.
Anthropic’s millionaire factory promises to expand the group of tech buyers, who range from senior staff at major AI labs to founders who have sold their startups, with budgets that range from £2m to £40m, Eccles says.
Tech’s wave of wealth has already reshaped Silicon Valley – notably in San Francisco – driving up demand for already scarce housing as young entrepreneurs and engineers became millionaires overnight. Now, that money is washing up on British shores too.
Anthropic, which employs about 5,000 people worldwide, has more than 200 employees in the UK. The company, founded in San Francisco in 2021, has announced plans to expand its presence in London, with a new office that is capable of accommodating up to 800 people.
The company’s UK filings show that it spent £24.1m employing an average of 43 staff in 2024 alone – a mean average of £560,000 per person. Job listings this year have advertised base salaries of up to £630,000 before stock options for research engineers.
Salaries across Britain’s AI sector are flying: OpenAI’s staff in London each received £2.3m on average last year – about 58 times the median UK full-time employee earnings. That puts them on par with partners at top law firms such as Linklaters and Clifford Chance, and ahead of some bankers in the City.
UK-based investors in these companies are also watching the value of their stakes grow at breakneck speed. Alex Gerko, the billionaire founder of the trading firm XTX and an early investor in Anthropic via the venture arms of the business, is expected to make hundreds of millions of pounds in paper gains when the company joins the stock market this week.
The flush of technology cash is already evident in London’s commercial property market. First, a wave of startups led to Shoreditch being nicknamed Silicon Roundabout , before tech firms began expanding across the capital. Now, US AI firms are expanding at pace in the UK, clustering tightly inside the King’s Cross “knowledge quarter” where Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta all work a stone’s throw from each other.
They have followed in the footsteps of Demis Hassabis , a totemic figure in AI’s breakthrough era who co-founded DeepMind in 2010 and sold it to Google for £400m four years later. He was one of the first to set up in the north London enclave. Isomorphic Labs, his AI drug discovery startup that is also now owned by the Google parent Alphabet, is in the area.
The AI gold rush is already being felt at the highest end of London’s housing market. Although tech bosses may be younger than the sector’s traditional client base, agents report that interest – while spread across London – includes plenty of familiar wealthy haunts.
In February, the Times reported that Igor Babuschkin, the billionaire co-founder of Elon Musk’s AI venture xAI, had bought a £57m penthouse overlooking Hyde Park, in one of the biggest deals in the city this year.
Meanwhile, Providence House, the Reform UK treasurer Nick Candy’s former mansion on the grounds of the Royal Hospital Chelsea in London, was reportedly sold for £270m to the founder of the quantitative investment firm Quadrature Capital, Suneil Setiya. Aidan Devane, the chief executive of the firm, attributed its success partly to its proximity to AI labs in the city, telling the Financial Times: “We are probably in the golden age of London quant.”
Tech wealth, increasingly generated by gains in the AI sector, “has become a force at the very top of the prime central London market”, according to the super-prime estate agent Beauchamp Estates, which has a portfolio including a £42m sub-penthouse overlooking Hyde Park.
Jeremy Gee, a managing director at Beauchamp, says inquiries from tech and AI buyers have risen noticeably over the past year. “Some are international buyers, principally from the US, but a growing number are based here in London,” he says, adding that many have amassed their fortunes with remarkable speed.
“They tend to be younger, they move quickly and they are very clear about what they want. Location and quality matter most and they will pay a premium for something genuinely special,” he says. “London offers culture, history, world-class schools and a growing AI community of its own.”
Even the traditional bastions of old British money are adapting. According to Shona Baijal, the managing director of wealth at Coutts, the private bank long associated with the British aristocracy, the tech and AI sectors are increasingly a source of new clients. One of the key challenges, she says, is helping young entrepreneurs who are coming into vast amounts of wealth very quickly.
“A lot of people feel overwhelmed,” she says. “We have to discuss the emotional aspects of what it means to come into wealth. We might say: you’ve come into the money, but do not rush to do anything.”
Coutts found last month that eight out of 10 properties in London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods – such as Mayfair, Belgravia and Knightsbridge – now sell below asking price.
But sellers and property agents hoping the AI industry may ride to London’s rescue face a glaring problem: much of these new AI fortunes remains on paper.
At founder level, many are “paper rich, cash poor”, Baijal says – meaning until they sell their businesses or their shares vest, their wealth is largely theoretical.
At the same time, Britain’s wider economy is growing more reliant on the sector’s momentum. Last week, official figures showed that the UK economy grew by 0.7% in the third quarter, its fastest expansion in two and a half years, almost entirely due to strong and widespread growth in services, led by the IT sector. Separate analysis by Bloomberg found that roughly a quarter of UK economic growth this year had been powered by AI.
That dependence makes the prospect of an AI bubble bursting all the more dangerous. There have been months of warnings over the valuations of AI companies, and there has been a groundswell of public opposition to datacentre construction and worries around AI safety.
Investors were reminded again of the fragility of the AI trade last week after a scandal involving extramarital affairs and an alleged Chinese spy sent shares in one of the most valuable AI companies in the US, the chip designer Nvidia, tumbling.
Other market indicators have been flashing warning lights. This year one popular measure used by investors to assess whether a market is overvalued – the CAPE, or cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings, ratio – rose to its highest level since 2000 , showing that the US stock market was unusually highly valued compared with its profits. That was before the Anthropic’s blockbuster debut.
For now, the AI boom’s physical footprint is unmistakable. In San Francisco, the average one-bedroom property now rents for $4,400 a month, up more than 25% from last year and nearly three times the US average. Landlords have been trying to capitalise on the boom, particularly in areas closest to the offices of the biggest AI companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.

Meta , Instagram'ın mesajlaşma deneyimini ayrı bir uygulamaya taşıyan Direct isimli yeni uygulamasını test etmeye başladı. Şimdilik yalnızca Türkiye ve Tayland'da kullanıma sunulan Direct, kullanıcıların Instagram hesabına sahip olmadan da mesajlaşabilmesine imkan tanıyor.
Direct'in arayüzü, Instagram'ın mevcut mesaj kutusuna oldukça benziyor. Instagram hesabıyla giriş yapan kullanıcıların mevcut sohbetleri yeni uygulamaya aktarılıyor. Uygulamada sohbetlere özel arka planlar oluşturma ve Instagram'ın kısa durum güncellemeleri sunan Notlar özelliği de bulunuyor.
Direct'i kullanmak için Instagram hesabına sahip olmanız gerekmiyor. Kullanıcılar e-posta adresleri veya telefon numaralarıyla yeni bir Direct hesabı oluşturabiliyor. Ancak Instagram hesabı olmadan uygulamayı kullananların, sohbet başlatmak istedikleri kişileri Instagram kullanıcı adı veya QR kod aracılığıyla manuel olarak eklemesi gerekiyor.
Meta, Instagram'daki bazı güvenlik özelliklerini Direct'e de taşıyor. Buna göre kullanıcılar, bağlantı kurmadıkları kişilerle doğrudan sohbet başlatamıyor. Şirket ayrıca genç kullanıcılarla gerçekleştirilebilecek uygunsuz etkileşimleri tespit etmek ve bunlara müdahale etmek için teknolojiden yararlanacağını belirtiyor. Ancak bu sistemin nasıl çalışacağına ilişkin ayrıntılar henüz resmi olarak paylaşılmadı. Meta'nın ebeveyn denetimi araçlarını kullanan aileler ise gençlerin Direct üzerinden kimlerle mesajlaştığını ve uygulamada ne kadar zaman geçirdiğini takip edebilecek.
Direct'in ortaya çıkışı, Instagram'ın son yıllarda giderek daha fazla mesajlaşma odaklı bir platforma dönüşmesi açısından da dikkat çekici. Instagram'ın 2017'nin Aralık ayında mesajlaşma özelliğini Direct adı altında ayrı bir uygulama olarak yayınladığını hatırlatalım . Şirket, 2019 yılında Direct uygulamasını kapatma kararı almıştı. 2020 yılında ise Instagram Threads, Direct'in yerini almaya hazırlanmaktaydı .
Öte yandan Instagram Başkanı Adam Mosseri , daha önce mesajlaşmanın Instagram'da en fazla kullanılan özelliklerden biri olduğunu birçok kez dile getirmişti. Buna karşın Mosseri, geçmişte Instagram mesaj kutusunun Threads'e taşınması fikrine mesafeli yaklaşmış ve aynı kişilere birden fazla uygulama üzerinden ulaşmanın gereksiz bir deneyim yaratabileceğini belirtmişti.
Meta'nın şimdi Instagram mesajlaşmasını tamamen ayrı bir uygulamayla test etmesi bu açıdan önemli bir strateji değişikliğine işaret ediyor. Özellikle Direct'in Instagram hesabı olmayan kişiler tarafından da kullanılabilmesi, uygulamanın daha geniş bir kapsamlı bir mesajlaşma hizmetine dönüşmesinin önünü açabilir.
Bu durum Direct'i aynı zamanda Meta'nın diğer mesajlaşma platformu WhatsApp ile kısmen karşı karşıya getirebilir. Direct'in WhatsApp'ın yerini alması pek mümkün olmasa da, Instagram kullanmayan kişilerin de uygulamaya katılabilmesi, Meta'nın mesajlaşma ekosistemi içinde kullanıcıların geçirdiği zamanı farklı uygulamalar arasında yeniden dağıtabilir.
Meta, Direct'i şu aşamada yalnızca Türkiye ve Tayland 'da gerçekleştirilen bir test olarak konumlandırıyor. Şirket uygulamanın başka ülkelere açılıp açılmayacağına ilişkin henüz bir takvim paylaşmış değil. Testin başarılı olması halinde Direct'in daha geniş bir kullanıcı kitlesine sunulması gündeme gelebilir.

Uber , hizmet aldığı teknoloji şirketlerinden Fireworks A I 'da yaşanan siber saldırı nedeniyle yaklaşık 150 bin kişinin kişisel bilgilerinin çalındığını açıkladı. Saldırganlar, Fireworks AI'ın sistemlerine sızarak Uber'in verilerine erişti. Çalınan bilgiler arasında sürücülerin adları, adresleri, doğum tarihleri ve ehliyet numaraları bulunuyor.
Uber, 9 Ekim'de Fireworks AI'dan saldırıyla ilgili bilgi aldığını ve olaydan etkilenen kişileri bilgilendirmeye başladığını belirtti. Oregon Başsavcılığına sunulan bildirimde, saldırıdan etkilenen kişi sayısının 149 bin 346 olduğu açıklandı. Şirket, etkilenen sürücülerin sayısına ilişkin ayrıca bir açıklama yapmadı.
TechCrunch'ın haberine göre saldırının gerçekleştiği Fireworks AI, geliştiricilerin açık ağırlıklı yapay zeka modellerini kullanmasını sağlayan bir teknoloji şirketi. Fireworks AI, geçen ay bilgisayar korsanlarının sistemlerine girdiğini ve müşterilerine ait bazı bilgileri ele geçirdiğini duyurmuştu. Notion ve Cursor da aynı saldırıda verilerinin çalındığını doğruladı.
Uber, Fireworks AI sistemlerine yönelik yetkisiz erişimleri tespit etmek için güvenlik uyarıları kullandığını ancak saldırganların şirketin kendi erişim bilgilerini kullanması nedeniyle herhangi bir uyarı almadığını açıkladı . Fireworks AI ise saldırının maddi kazanç elde etmeyi amaçlayan bir siber suç grubu tarafından gerçekleştirildiğini belirtti. Şirkete göre saldırganlar, büyük dil modellerine (LLM) erişim sağlayan çalıntı erişim anahtarlarını satmayı hedefliyor. Ancak henüz bilinen hiçbir siber suç grubu saldırının sorumluluğunu üstlenmedi.
Öte yandan bu olay, Uber'in bu yıl yaşadığı bilinen ikinci veri ihlali oldu. Şirket, ağustos ayında kamyon taşımacılığı hizmeti Uber Freight'in de bir siber saldırıyla karşı karşıya kaldığını açıklamıştı.

Bank of America, Chase, US Bank, Wells Fargo and Truist were listed by users who have been experiencing issues
Customers reported service outages and difficulty accessing their online accounts at several major US banks and the money transfer service Zelle on Monday after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.
Chase said the technical problems were not a systemic issue and were not the result of a cyber-attack, and that it was working to bring banking services back online.
“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” a Chase spokesperson said in a statement. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.”
The disruption comes after a major outage by Microsoft that began on Thursday and lasted into the next day, which crippled a host of services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot. The outage had serious repercussions for millions of people and organizations all over the world, including schools, hospitals, businesses, courts, banks, prisons, police forces and governments.
Microsoft said it had resolved the issue and restored service by Saturday, also issuing an apology. The office software giant did not attribute the blackout to a cybersecurity breach, identifying in an initial report on Monday that a combination of a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections, and server capacity sparked the outage.
Also on Friday, ageing equipment led to a temporary grounding of all commercial airplanes in the US, sparking travel chaos as thousands of flights were delayed or canceled. The Trump administration later said the four-hour ground stop stemmed from routine maintenance.
At a briefing on Saturday, US transportation secretary Sean Duffy said the outage began after “a contractor was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire … to fiber” and a newly installed router “started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system”.
The FAA, he said, was still working to determine whether the fault was “incompetence” by the contractor, or “a faulty router”.
Monday’s technical issues seem to center on Chase customers and customers at other banks trying to transact with Chase. Those banks, including Bank of America and Citigroup, were not having issues with their banking services.
A spokesman for US Bank said its systems are not directly affected but that “clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”
Zelle, the peer-to-peer payment system that major US banks use to allow customers to send money near-instantly to friends and family, is owned by Arizona-based Early Warning Services, which in turn is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, US Bank and Wells Fargo .
A spokesperson for Early Warning Services said the Zelle network was fully operational. “An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers,” they said.
Some Chase customers received a message that said: “Some services aren’t available. We’re working on them. Please try back later.”

Thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, have reported trouble accessing services.
Chase Bank - the largest banking institution in the US - said a "software bug" in its hardware systems may have been behind the glitch and noted the impacts may have affected other banks. It added the issue was "temporary" and not "systemic" or "cyber-related".
Problems appeared to be easing for many customers by early Monday evening.
The issue comes after a string of unrelated technical problems, including a massive Microsoft outage , a network failure that grounded all US flights , and United Airlines reporting a "widespread system outage".
Problems started on Monday afternoon. There were almost 5,000 reports of problems with Chase Bank's services, according to the Downdetector website.
Clients reported issues accessing their online accounts, viewing balances and performing transactions, like bank transfers and wire transfers, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.
A Chase Bank customer in Texas told the outlet that he could not deposit a check at a Dallas branch on Monday, reporting that he was told his transaction could not be completed. He said a bank teller told the customer in front of him that the "system was down" but did not provide additional details.
Microsoft says services fully restored after day-long global outage
Microsoft outage 'stark reminder' of how much we rely on tech
Chase Bank told its customers that "some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete" but they still had "access to their accounts and funds".
The bank, a subsidiary of JP Morgan Chase, serves more than 86m customers at 5,000 branches across the US, as well as 7.4m small businesses, according to the company's webpage. It is also the top credit card issuer in the US.
The exact nature of the bug was unclear. The BBC has contacted Chase Bank.
Bank of America customers had issues at ATMs and using mobile banking services online, while US Bank customers reported issues with their online accounts and the bank's mobile app, CBS reported.
Customers using another institution, US Bank, also reported issues transferring funds and Wells Fargo customers said they had problems signing into their accounts, getting account balances and making transactions.
US Bank said some its systems were not directly affected but clients using the Zelle, a digital payment platform, received error messages saying their payments could not be sent.
Zelle has said its service is "operating as it should" and issues at other banks could be affecting payments.
Customers also reported issues with Truist, PNC and Capital One but all these companies told the BBC they have not been impacted.
As of 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT), Chase, Bank of America and US Bank had seen a fall in the number of reported outages.
Just as the banking issue affected US customers on Monday, United Airlines confirmed a "widespread system outage", which it described as "a technology issue affecting departing flights".
The Chicago-based airline did not say what is believed to have caused the issue, but a spokesperson said it is not related to cybersecurity.
The issue did not appear to be affecting any other airlines.
The United issue is separate from the one that hit the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) , but comes as other industries report different outages around the US.
On Friday, the FAA issued a rare nationwide a ground stop, halting all US air travel due to a telecommunication and network upgrade issues.
The halt lasted just over four hours, but the knock-on effect continues to snarl US air travel.

texts.https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw77:
The Crimea bridge (pictured in 2023) has been repeatedly targeted by Ukraine
A key bridge linking occupied Crimea and Russia is closed after reports a Ukrainian strike inflicted major damage, during a night in which the warring countries both targeted major crossings.
A former adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky shared images purporting to show that a section of the Crimea bridge - also known as the Kerch Bridge - had collapsed into the water.
Meanwhile, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Northern and Southern bridges, important routes over the Dnipro River, were closed after Russian ballistic missile strikes.
Those attacks came a day after Ukraine began its most recent attempt to disable the Crimea bridge, a prized Kremlin asset seen as a symbol of Russia's occupation.
Two people were killed in that strike overnight on Sunday, the Russian-installed governor of Crimea said.
Former Ukrainian adviser Anton Gerashchenko shared images and video footage appearing to show extensive damage to the bridge from the latest strike, with a support arch and road section seen protruding from the water below. BBC News has not independently verified those images.
The bridge, which has come under repeated attack by Ukrainian forces, was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014, and was personally opened by Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2018.
While Ukraine has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the Crimea bridge is an attempt do increase the political cost on Putin.
The severity of the latest strike on the route, which is protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences, is still not fully clear - but Russian state media reported a meeting was due to be held on Tuesday to discuss the situation.
Crimea's Moscow-backed governor Sergei Aksyonov confirmed on Telegram that traffic over the bridge had been suspended.
The Northern Bridge (pictured in October) is closed after being targeted again by Russia
Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between the Chinese, US and Russian leaders in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.
Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground subway services were damaged in the overnight attacks, officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Residents of Kyiv typically shelter in the city's underground stations during air raids.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
These latest Russian strikes will cause major disruption, with traffic already reportedly building in the capital.
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the Cherkast region, according to local officials.
The latest round of tit-for-tat strikes came after US, Ukrainian and European officials held talks on ways to facilitate "direct engagement" between Russia and Europe to end the war.
Following Monday's meeting, US envoy Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, said the US was committed to providing Ukraine with a "strong, credible security guarantees", as well as a path towards EU membership.
He added that Nato "will remain a critical pillar of European security", and that preparations are underway for a further multilateral meeting "in the near future".
Zelensky said that the meeting was "difficult", adding that more needed to be done to support Ukraine's defence against Russian ballistic missile strikes, which he said were being provided by North Korea.
The Ukrainian president has long called for European nations to be included in any peace talks, which he argues is necessary because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the EU.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian officials said the final death toll from a Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian village of Kamyshuvakha earlier this month had reached 72.
Four people are still considered missing after the bombing, which Ukrainian officials said was one of the deadliest individual attacks since the start of the war in 2022.
Footage, from a camera on one of the killed police officers, showed residents going to an underground shelter after the initial attack on 2 November. Soon after a blast is heard and flames are seen as the shelter is hit.
Ukrainian police said of those killed were police officers, "staff of the gymnasium, utility workers and medical personnel".
Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

Ukraine says bodycam video shows deadly Russian double-tap bombing
Zelensky welcomes US bringing Europe into Russia-Ukraine peace talks

A Chase software bug disrupted US banking transactions and delayed some Zelle payments. Here’s what happened.
Thousands of customers across the United States reported problems accessing banking services and making payments after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase disrupted transactions involving other banks.
The problems on Monday affected customers at several major financial institutions, including Wells Fargo and Bank of America, while some users also reported delays with Zelle payments.
So, what caused the US bank outages, which banks were affected, and have services returned to normal?
Thousands of US customers reported problems accessing online banking services after JPMorgan Chase said a software issue caused knock-on effects for transactions involving other banks.
The disruption extended to customers of at least five other banks, who reported issues accessing services and completing transactions.
According to the French news agency AFP, reports on outage-tracking Downdetector peaked at around 2pm Eastern Standard Time (19:00 GMT) before declining later in the day.
“JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system – it is not cyber-related,” said Joe Evangelisti, spokesperson for the bank.
Customers of several major US banks reported problems on Monday.
These included JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, US Bank, Truist and Capital One.
However, not all the banks reported problems with their own systems.
Chase confirmed experiencing technical problems, while US Bank said its own systems were not directly affected. Capital One and Truist also said their services were operating normally.
JPMorgan Chase said that a software bug in its internal hardware systems had slowed transaction processing and may have delayed transactions involving other banks.
Some customers said they were not able to access accounts and funds, although Chase said customers continued to have access.
The bank stressed that the disruption was not systemic and that other banks may have experienced delays when processing transactions involving Chase.
Chase is the consumer banking division of JPMorgan Chase, which holds the most assets of any US bank. It handles payments involving other financial institutions, meaning a technical problem at Chase can also delay transactions for customers at other banks, even if those banks’ systems are operating normally.
“This is not a systemic issue – other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,” Evangelisti added.
Zelle is the peer-to-peer third-party payment system that major US banks use to allow customers to send money to friends and family at near-instant speed.
It is owned by Early Warning Services, an Arizona-based company that is itself owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, US Bank and Wells Fargo.
In the US, some customers also reported problems sending and receiving payments through Zelle.
The company said that customers access Zelle through participating banks and credit unions so technical problems at those institutions can affect the ability to make a payment even if Zelle’s own systems are fully operational.
US Bank said its systems were not directly affected but warned that customers sending or receiving Zelle payments involving other financial institutions could experience delays.
JPMorgan Chase said that transactions were processing normally again following the disruption.
A Chase spokesperson said that shortly after close of business on Monday, at approximately 6:30pm (23:30 GMT), transactions were posting normally, according to NBC News.
However, the restoration of Chase’s transaction processing does not necessarily mean every delayed payment has been completed.
There is no confirmed connection between Monday’s outages and the recent Microsoft outage and disruptions impacting the US government’s transport agency, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).
The banking problems followed two major incidents in the US last week.
On Thursday, Microsoft experienced a widespread outage that disrupted services including Outlook. A day later, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop following a technical failure affecting air traffic control communications.
The incidents had different reported causes. JPMorgan Chase said its disruption was due to a software bug, while the FAA disruption involved malfunctioning equipment.
However, Jody Westby, CEO of cybersecurity advisory firm Global Cyber Risk, told Al Jazeera that the series of incidents raised questions about the reliability and security of critical infrastructure.
“I think it’s very concerning that everyone’s just jumping to the conclusion it’s a technical issue, it’s a software bug, it was old equipment,” she said.
“I don’t think that any of that is a complete explanation the public deserves.”
Westby said she believed more detailed investigations were needed.
“My concern is that we are not diligently looking into these incidents and analysing them, and even with a global working group to make sure that we can determine whether there are any correlations.”

Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals.
Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements.
The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin.
Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said.
The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually junked by the incoming Labour government in 2024 .
Downing Street has not ruled out the UK joining the scheme, saying they will watch it "with interest".
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said the plan to open a centre in Rwanda had no "future or humanity", according to AFP news agency.
"I don't see any future or humanity in that. It's not the solution," Sanchez told the Spanish broadcaster Telecinco, AFP reported.
The five countries say the plan to send migrants abroad is in line with EU and international law, but human rights bodies say it could violate migrant rights.
The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of hubs outside of the bloc.
In a joint press conference in Vienna on Monday, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said the five countries wanted to relieve European asylum systems and stop traffickers arranging deadly trips across the Mediterranean.
In a written statement, the Dutch government said the five countries will "only return single men" as part of the first phase of the deal, adding that the focus for the Netherlands "will be on persons from countries of origin in the same region as Rwanda".
Once in Rwanda, people will be able to integrate into society, which means they will have the right of residence, as well as access to education, healthcare, the labour market and the legal system.
Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the country is commmited to working with European partners to provide a "safe, legal and dignified solution for migrants".
He added that they would also work on "correcting the global imbalance in economic opportunities", which he called a "key driver of irregular migration".
Ahead of the announcement, diplomatic sources told the AFP news agency the hub is expected to initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending about 20 migrants.
The United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role.
"IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts," an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries "on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms".
With elections approaching in several EU nations, administrations have been under pressure to show they can control migration.
Concerns around security, struggling economies and disillusionment with governing parties have all had a major role in shaping attitudes towards people leaving their home countries .
Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher Clementine de Montjoye said the choice of Rwanda would be a cause of concern as it had a "well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention" and support for armed rebels in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo.
"Paying Kigali to host a deportation programme would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad."
The independent EU Agency for Fundamental Rights argued any third country hosting a return hub should "respect fundamental rights", including that people should not be sent to a country where they face serious risk of persecution.
The agency added that unaccompanied children should not be sent to a return hub, which the Dutch government has confirmed will not take place.
According to the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, there were almost 110,000 irregular border crossings into the EU in the first 10 months of 2026, which represents a 29% decrease compared to the previous year.
In October, about 18,100 crossings were detected, which is about 6% less than October 2025 but 22% more than in September "largely because of a sharp rise in arrivals on the Western African route to the Canary Islands".

Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’
Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.
The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.
In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.
Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.
In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.
Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania , it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.
The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.
The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe .
Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said it was “a huge breakthrough”.
The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”
Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”
Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government , which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.
Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, said on Monday the move had no “future or humanity”. “I don’t see any future or humanity in that. It’s not the solution,” Sanchez, an outspoken defender of immigration in a Europe that has tilted to the right in recent years, told Telecinco television.
The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She said: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union , with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”
Alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, said it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.
“On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.
Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.
Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.

Campaigners call for reopening of high-speed Eurostar stations and new infrastructure for London St Pancras
Britain should throw its weight behind international rail services to reset the UK-EU relationship, transport campaigners have urged the prime minister.
A coalition of groups has called on Andy Burnham to commit to reopening high-speed stations for Eurostar and other services in Kent, and to support new infrastructure for passengers at London St Pancras and for rail freight.
The call came alongside research showing that annual rail passenger numbers through the Channel tunnel could more than double in five years and hit 28 million by 2040.
The report said that planned increases in services and routes , including competition to Eurostar from new operators and significant investment in rolling stock, should drive demand for international rail travel, but that the government needed to help realise the potential.
A letter to Burnham from the Campaign for Better Transport, co-signed by sustainable transport groups and train operators, said the numbers would come “only if a strategy is put in place and the barriers to growth are unlocked”. The campaigners urged him to tackle high fares and border delays and invest in more depot and station capacity.
Ben Plowden, the chief executive of the Campaign for Better Transport , said: “The Channel tunnel is one of Britain’s greatest, underused transport assets. Improving our international rail network would give people a genuine alternative to flying, making international travel more affordable and accessible, and delivering major benefits for the economy and the environment.”
According to research by the Transport and Environment (T&E) thinktank, three times as many Britons support expanding international rail rather than airports. Labour has approved expansion at London’s Stansted, Luton and Gatwick airports, although, significantly, Burnham has not expressed support for Heathrow’s third runway.
Georgia Whitaker, a rail campaigns manager at T&E, said: “If the EU and UK want to get back on track, ensuring the Channel tunnel is no longer half-used is a no-brainer.”
Gareth Williams, the general secretary of Eurostar , said: “The UK needs a big picture plan to unleash international rail growth. There is a real opportunity to deliver economic benefits through rail and to provide low-carbon connections, including direct routes as far afield as Germany and Switzerland. To get there, there’s a need to be ambitious about infrastructure investment – particularly in stations and depots that are fit for the future.”
The letter calls on Burnham to open Stratford International station in east London as a second gateway into the capital, something the government committed to providing funding for in the autumn budget.
It also urged him to commit to reopening international services at Ashford and Ebbsfleet International stations. The letter is signed by Eurostar, despite the current cross-Channel operator having deemed the Kent stations commercially unviable.
A strategic approach to international rail should mean more investment, the report said, but it also pointed to “proportionate and efficient border and security arrangements”, better connections and integrated ticketing.
The campaigners also suggested levying more taxes on aviation to reflect the climate impact of short-haul flying compared with rail.
A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “We also want to see a thriving, competitive international rail market that gives passengers more choice and supports economic growth.
“That’s why we’re supporting industry and local partners to deliver international services at Stratford International, Ebbsfleet and Ashford, and are exploring options for new international rail depot capacity.”

Prime Minister Andy Burnham says UK lost more than it gained after its divorce from the bloc.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the Brexit promise failed to deliver for the United Kingdom and that the country needs to reset its relationship with the European Union to combat growing global isolationism.
During a speech at the Lord Mayor’s Banquet in London on Monday, Burnham compared the outcome of Britain’s divorce from the EU, triggered by a 2016 referendum, to the Hans Christian Andersen fairy tale “The Emperor’s New Clothes”, in which no one is willing to tell the ruler that he is, in fact, naked.
“I do try to say things as I see them,” Burnham said. “And to be frank, we have lost more than we have gained in the last 10 years. The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain.”
The remarks come ahead of a UK-EU summit in Brussels on Friday, which Burnham said could deliver “real improvements in people’s everyday lives in areas of the country that have felt neglected for too long”.
Any deal, he said, would have to pass three tests: it would have to be consistent with Labour’s manifesto and red lines, improve the Brexit deal to align with what people voted for in 2016 and pass his Makerfield Test, his benchmark for ensuring real improvements for people in parts of the UK that have long felt neglected.
The meeting is a key step in his pledge to reset relations with the 27-nation bloc a decade after the UK voted to leave and six years after its 2020 departure.
The UK is expected to seal a deal on trading food and drink, and make agreements on energy and emissions and a plan to let young people work for limited periods across Britain and the EU.
Burnham said the promise of the pro-Brexit campaign that Britain would “take back control” of its borders, laws and economy had not been delivered. Trade with EU countries has dropped sharply, and estimates of the economic damage range from 4 percent to 8 percent of the UK’s gross domestic product, he said.
Seeking to draw a line under a decade of political turmoil that has made him Britain’s seventh prime minister since 2016, Burnham said the UK was back on the world stage. He argued the country is well positioned to lead in an era of renewed international cooperation because of its experience since 2016.
“Brexit was the first domino to fall in a global move towards more isolationism and protectionism,” he said. “It is exactly what our enemies wanted. Russia wanted disunity within NATO and a weaker Europe.”
Burnham said that he will open a discussion with EU partners on Britain’s long-term relationship with the bloc soon after the Brussels summit. His spokesperson Tom Wells said on Monday that “no assumptions are being made” and “the British public will be the boss of any outcome”.
Until the next national election, Burnham remains bound by the pledge of Keir Starmer, whom he replaced as centre-left Labour Party leader and prime minister, not to rejoin the bloc’s tariff-free customs union or frictionless single market for goods, services and workers.
Erasing that pledge would reignite a subject that split the country: the 2016 referendum vote was 52 percent in favour of leaving the EU and 48 percent in support of remaining.

A student with near-perfect scores on two tests has confessed to using artificial intelligence.
South Korea is racing to fix potential security gaps in upcoming exams after a top scorer on a national test admitted to using artificial intelligence to cheat.
Prime Minister Han Seok-sook called an emergency meeting on Monday, where the education minister was tasked with enforcing new anti-cheating measures ahead of high-pressure annual national college entrance exams known as “Suneung” this week.
The scandal began after speculation mounted over a student’s near-perfect scores on two separate exams that contained hundreds of questions.
Now, authorities say cheaters using high-tech gadgets could face criminal prosecution if caught.
In a statement last week, the prime minister said her government “will prepare thoroughly in advance and closely oversee the process until the very end to ensure the college entrance exam is conducted fairly and stably”.
In a video published online on Sunday, the student, wearing a mask, admitted to using a miniature camera and AI during the exam for aspiring tax accountants.
Identified as Han Won-seok by South Korean media, the student had taken exams in April and July and answered nearly all questions correctly, raising concerns about potential cheating and prompting investigations.
“I cheated using electronic devices and generative AI. My passing the exam with the top score was not the result of fair effort,” he said in the YouTube video.
He explained that he took photos of the exam questions with the mini camera and sent them to an AI tool. He also said he used a smartphone.
The student said he had submitted a written confession detailing his process to the Seoul police. He also warned future cheaters to reconsider.
“I’m going to tell the investigators everything, so I hope you don’t think that you won’t get caught,” he said.
The prime minister has called for his results to be invalidated and for him to be banned from national examinations.
The case has triggered uproar in South Korea, where notoriously difficult tests determine students’ life trajectories.
Many spend much of their high school years preparing to pass entrance exams, particularly the Suneung, or the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), which lasts for nearly 10 hours. Flights are suspended to allow total concentration during the exam’s English listening segment, and drivers are asked not to honk for the half-an-hour it takes.
On Monday, Minister of Education Choi Kyo-jin said new measures would be instituted, including the inspection of glasses worn by students.
He also said cheating with smart devices could carry criminal punishment.
The ministry has in recent weeks said it would pursue criminal prosecution for cheating during the annual college entrance exam. It also said it was seeking to extend the one-year exam ban for those caught using smart devices to three years.
There will be “a thorough inspection of all glasses in each test session to ensure a fair and safe testing environment”, the minister said.
The case has revealed the risks AI could pose to exams as smart gadgets make cheating easier, and as authorities appear to be playing catch-up on how the new tools are being deployed.
It could especially affect Asian countries like South Korea, reputed for conducting arduous exams with strict anti-cheating protocols meant to ensure fairness.
Reports of students using AI-powered smart glasses that allow them to look at questions and see responses immediately are becoming common.
A South Korean education official said students likely enter AI prompts beforehand and activate the glasses during tests.
Early iterations of smart glasses featured identifiable cameras in their frames, but the devices are increasingly inconspicuous, making them difficult to detect.
In October, three students in South Korea were caught using smart glasses during tests at universities in Seoul.
In Taiwan, the National Taiwan University disqualified a student in June from medical school entrance exams for allegedly using AI smart glasses to cheat.
Authorities are promising stricter measures. In July, South Korea’s education authorities banned smart glasses from exams and said they will deploy one dedicated person per 1,312 CSAT test sites to inspect eyewear.
Seoul is also mulling introducing technology to detect advanced gadgets on students, including radio-frequency detectors. Public Wi-Fi, officials say, could be disabled at test sites too.
Chinese authorities are likewise tightening measures for the competitive college entry, or Gaokao, exam by equipping testing sites with intelligent security gates to detect smart glasses and other gadgets.

Gareth Bale (left) and Cristiano Ronaldo spent five trophy-laden years together at Real Madrid
Portugal are just one match into life after Cristiano Ronaldo, a footballing titan whose 23-year international career transformed the game in his homeland.
On Tuesday, they visit Wales, who are nearly four years into a similar adjustment after the retirement of their own icon, Gareth Bale.
History might suggest these two teams belong to different echelons of the sport. But in terms of individual players defining entire nations, Wales and Portugal share a profound connection.
Their records only tell half the story. Ronaldo and Bale scored more goals and won more caps than any other man to represent Portugal or Wales. In Ronaldo's case, more than any other man in the world.
What the two represented for their respective countries went beyond their remarkable statistics, though.
Ronaldo led Portugal to their first title at Euro 2016, beating Bale's Wales in a semi-final and ending a momentous Welsh journey in what was their first appearance at a major tournament for 58 years.
Both players gave their countries countless memorable moments, and not only on the international stage.
Former Real Madrid team-mates, Ronaldo and Bale won four and five Champions Leagues respectively, a combined five La Liga titles and a plethora of other team and individual accolades.
Whenever they held trophies aloft, you could bet they would be carrying, or often wearing, the national flags of Portugal and Wales – global ambassadors.
"You're losing an icon of the national team," says Wales captain Ben Davies, Bale's former team-mate and part of the Welsh defence which faced Ronaldo in what proved to be his final international appearance two months ago.
"But it's an opportunity for other players to stand up and try to take that limelight. We've had boys who've really stepped up in that time after we lost probably Wales' greatest player.
As secure as their legendary status might be, there are telling differences between the two.
When Bale announced his retirement aged 33 in January 2023, he did so because he acknowledged his once otherworldly powers were fading and he felt Wales needed to plan for the future.
Reserved by nature, Bale could not avoid an outpouring of adulation, but he tried to depart as quietly as he could.
By contrast, Ronaldo's exit earlier this month was messy, acrimonious and, according to some, long overdue for the 41-year-old.
He walked out of a Portugal camp in September after being told he would not start a Nations League match against Denmark, resulting in a £215 fine and 30-day suspension.
Without knowing beforehand that the Wales game earlier that month would be his last, Ronaldo did not get the send-off he would have wanted.
"I'm grateful that we got to see the longevity of a true great who's had one of the biggest impacts in football," says Wales head coach Craig Bellamy.
"He's left a mark on football that will live forever. I'm grateful I got to see him and I'm grateful I got to coach against him."
Glittering and record-breaking as Ronaldo's international career undoubtedly was, the final few years were somewhat strained.
At this summer's World Cup and other recent tournaments, his star was clearly on the wane, prompting some to question whether Portugal might be better off without him.
Some of their underwhelming performances with Ronaldo leading the attack may have backed up that view, but supporters of the five-time Ballon d'Or winner could point to Portugal's first game since his retirement – Saturday's 4-1 home defeat by Denmark – as a riposte.
"You were all having a go at him for playing and then as soon as he retires then suddenly it's all hell breaks loose," Bellamy adds.
"He is one of the best players that has ever played the game. We are all going to miss him.
"Portugal will be completely fine. Portugal are able to leave players who cost £80m to £100m out of their squad. They can pick 30, 40 players and be ridiculous. Before that you had Figo, you had Rui Costa, before that you had Eusebio.
"The game will move on, but I always feel we should celebrate him."
Bellamy makes an important point, highlighting arguably the biggest distinction between Portugal's prospects after Ronaldo's retirement and the task Wales have faced since Bale's departure.
Portugal's squad is among the best in the world, littered with world-class talent in every position, a true embarrassment of riches. As Bellamy says, they will be fine.
The current Wales squad, meanwhile, features four League One players and one on loan in the National League.
The two teams are in the same Nations League group but worlds apart.
While Bale was part of a wider golden generation, the fact that Wales have always had to rely on thinner resources than their rivals only added to the sense of wonder that they could produce this phenomenon.
The likes of Harry Wilson have taken their game to new levels since Bale's retirement but, as the Leeds United playmaker himself said earlier this year, nobody can replace Wales' greatest.
Nobody will claim to be able to replace Ronaldo either. In Portugal, he has an almost religious following.
In pure footballing terms, though, they have more than enough to fill the void. Four of this year's Ballon d'Or nominees were Portuguese.
The reigning Nations League champions travel to Cardiff on Tuesday shorn of an all-time great but still blessed with a galaxy of stars.
"Does it [Ronaldo's retirement] change how we approach the game? It doesn't, because it's just the level of quality you're up against," Bellamy says.
"They still have about 15 Champions League winners in the squad.
"They were fine before him, then they had a brilliant moment with him, and they'll be brilliant after it as well."

Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Ukrainian officials say is a symbolic blow to the Kremlin.

The latest drone and missile barrage appears to have succeeded, after months in which Ukrainian unmanned systems forces have systematically knocked out the peninsula’s multi-layered air defences.
The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed the bridge, which was temporarily closed on Monday, was no longer usable. “The enemy has once again attacked the Crimean Bridge. At the moment, traffic has been suspended,” he posted.

The US president oscillates between strike threats on Iran and insisting the war ‘militarily is effectively over’
A third US aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East, US Central Command said in a social media post on Monday, making a dramatic show of military might as Donald Trump keeps his options open for next steps in the Iran war.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt brings thousands of additional troops to the Middle East as Trump has oscillated between threatening additional large-scale strikes on Iran and insisting that the more than eight-month-old war “militarily is effectively over”.
The Roosevelt, along with its accompanying strike force, left San Diego in September. It joins the USS George HW Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller navy ships, which are in the region to maintain a naval blockade of Iranian shipping.
The George HW Bush arrived in the region in April, while the George Washington arrived in August. The navy previously had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April, for the first time since 2003.
In addition to the three aircraft carriers, the flotilla in the Arabian Sea now includes 13 destroyers, two cruisers and a littoral combat ship, according to the navy. Two more destroyers are in the Red Sea.
The Roosevelt had deployed along with the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group, which includes the USS John P Murtha and USS Anchorage amphibious landing ships and around 2,000 marines. Those ships have yet to make it to the region.
The third carrier arrived nearly two weeks after midterm elections that saw voters deliver major losses to Trump’s Republican party, driven in part by the unpopularity of the Iran war and its economic effects. The results led JD Vance to publicly break with Trump over the conflict, posting on social media that “the reason we lost is the war”.
Trump has insisted it was the right thing to do and has not ruled out restarting the conflict, which has been locked in a stalemate for months.
Last week, Trump warned Iran that the US military is “locked and loaded” and that the US was keeping an eye on Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to Iran’s nuclear program, for signs of activity.
“If something does not work out, I would not hesitate” to act, Trump told conservative broadcaster Hugh Hewitt on Thursday.
Yet, Trump also told reporters last week that he believed it was highly unlikely he would need to order new major strikes on Iran, declaring that the war “militarily is effectively over” after meeting with Qatar’s prime minister.
Trump also declared that the US no longer needs a deal with Tehran and told Vance – who was a chief negotiator in earlier ceasefire talks – instead to focus on the administration’s domestic anti-fraud campaign targeting Democratic-controlled cities and states.
Negotiations have stalled due to differences over Iran’s nuclear program, an issue that Trump insists be part of any deal meant to end the war. Iran wants the US first to agree to several core conditions, including lifting the naval blockade that is stopping its oil from getting to world markets.
In the meantime, a focal point of the simmering conflict remains the strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway where a fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war.
Commercial ships are still coming under attack or facing other risks, while the US has carried out limited strikes on Iranian targets near the strait and is helping guide vessels through the contested waters.
Iranian state TV, quoting the naval arm of Iran’s revolutionary guard and the army, warned shipping companies Monday that a US-supported route through the waterway is dangerous because of mines.
Mines have damaged six oil tankers since Sunday, polluting the strait’s coastlines, according to the revolutionary guard’s navy.
Separately, a projectile struck a tanker trying to transit through the strait, starting an engine room fire, but no casualties were reported, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organization said.
US Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, said it has redirected 150 merchant vessels and disabled five since June under the blockade.
Independent assessments from Lloyd’s List, a maritime tracking and analysis firm, show that traffic through the strait remains at less than a third of prewar levels.

Accusations of incompetence follow retreat of Riyadh-backed forces in effort to relieve siege of Taiz and protect Aden
Saudi Arabia has been accused by anti-Houthi forces over its military strategy after its Yemeni allies withdrew troops from the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and pulled back forces from parts of Marib in the central part of the country.
The Saudi-backed government explained the repositioning by saying the strategic priority was to break the attritional siege on Taiz , Yemen’s third city, and to protect Aden, the southern port city in which the Saudi-backed and UN-recognised government is now based.
Many blame the Houthi advance on the absence of a consolidated military command and control among the disparate forces backing the Aden-based government. Saudi Arabia responded to the setback by sidelining the commander of its Yemen coalition, Lt Gen Fahd bin Abdulaziz al-Salman, and replacing him with the chief of staff, Gen Fayyad bin Hamed bin Ruqad al-Ruwaili.
The Houthis’ steady advance towards the areas surrounding Bab al-Mandab, the narrow strait linking the Red Sea with the Indian Ocean on Yemen’s west coast, culminated on Sunday with a formal withdrawal of Yemen government forces, including some in the Southern Giants Brigades that had always been reluctant to defend territory outside the old southern Yemen. In 1990 Yemen had been divided in two, and many in the south want to return to a separated state.
The Saudi-backed government launched a fresh military campaign 42 days ago to drive the Houthis from Yemen but so far it has backfired.
The forces redeployed on Sunday have moved along the coast to al-Suqyah, 95 miles west of Aden, and inside the old Southern Yemen.
The retreat seems to be acknowledgment of Houthi resilience and is all the more remarkable given the Saudi air superiority. More than 300,000 Yemeni civilians have been displaced.
Amr al-Bidh, special representative of the exiled Southern Transitional Council (STC) leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, a separatist anti-Houthi force that is opposed by Saudi Arabia, accused the Saudis of incompetence – and in effect warned Riyadh that unless it became more open to a southern state it would lack the cohesive forces required to prevent the Houthis becoming a permanent security threat.
He said: “When there is no strategy and no plan, it is inevitable the Houthis would take advantage. The STC will defend the south to the last man but we are fighting with one hand behind our backs since January after Saudi Arabia attacks on the STC.
“The STC forces retain a credible capability on the ground. But we need practical and political support from the region to counter the Houthis and create the basis for a negotiated settlement, one in which the pathway towards southern independence is fully recognised. We cannot continue like this or else the Houthis will keep expanding.”
The breadth of support for the STC, backed by the United Arab Emirates, however, remains disputed. The movement suffered a near fatal setback in January and since then some of the Giants Brigades have switched to backing Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia continues in effect to keep as many as 10 STC leaders hostage in Riyadh, and has refused to let al-Zubaidi to return from exile in Abu Dhabi. Al-Bidh argued the priority should be defensive, avoiding counteroffensives that backfire, improving command and control, and widening the coalition.
Al-Bidh said reconciliation would require Riyadh to acknowledge the political declaration al-Zubaidi made about a timetable for a southern state in January, and that al-Zubaidi’s return would boost morale and help unify chaotic southern military factions.
He said a recent Yemeni government cabinet reshuffle, including a new information minister, was designed primarily to try draw southerners into fighting the Houthis and not to change policy toward the south.
He also urged the UK to use its diplomacy to bring in other actors rather than simply backing Riyadh. A group of southern Yemenis have written to the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, seeking a review of UK policy. “We recognise that the longstanding advice from your office is to continue following the Saudi line while calling for unity among the anti-Houthi forces,” the letter said. “But you must surely recognise that every time Britain calls for ‘the unity and territorial integrity of Yemen’, it is asking the southern people and their armed forces to fight for a political outcome in which they do not believe”.
The former US special envoy to Yemen Tim Lenderking said the US administration was treating Yemen like a sideshow adding “world powers do not understand the gravity of what it is at stake here”. He warned “the problem is only going to get bigger through apathy and lack of attention”.

Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee said there had been ‘no change in Russia’s position’ as Russia and Ukraine strike major infrastructure.
Ukraine has held new talks with United States and European officials on ending the war with Russia, hours before Kyiv’s mayor reported strikes on two bridges in the capital.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described Monday’s online discussions with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and European representatives as “not easy”. But he said participants had agreed to meet in Berlin with the “Coalition of the Willing”, a group of countries supporting Ukraine, as the US and Europe step up peace talks this week.
“Diplomatic processes are actively underway and we hope that these efforts will not be in vain,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly address.
He also warned that Ukrainian intelligence indicated Russia was preparing major strikes that night and throughout Tuesday.
Later on Monday, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said preliminary reports indicated that the North and South bridges across the Dnipro River had been hit. Air defence units were operating, and Reuters news agency witnesses heard a series of loud explosions.
Ukraine on Monday struck a key bridge and targeted oil refineries in what Russian defence ministry data indicated was the biggest overnight drone attack on Russia since the start of full-scale war in 2022. The Crimea Bridge was again struck overnight, with nearly 200 drones intercepted near Moscow, according to Telegram statements.
Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, said Washington was making progress towards an agreement in coordination with Russia, Ukraine and Europe.
“Important challenges remain, and a final agreement will require difficult decisions,” he wrote on X.
He said he and Witkoff had also spoken with Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov about the next steps. Their discussions included how to arrange direct engagement between Europe and Russia so each could hear the other’s concerns and proposals.
The exchanges followed last week’s talks in Abu Dhabi , where US, Ukrainian and Russian officials met together for the first time in nine months. Those negotiations produced an agreement on a prisoner exchange but no breakthrough on ending the war.
Witkoff and Kushner later met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and said European representatives would join the next round. On Monday, Moscow disputed that assertion.
Zelenskyy said representatives from France, Germany, Britain, Italy and Poland had participated fully in Monday’s discussion and would have the same representation in future meetings with Russian negotiators.
Ushakov said Russia had not agreed to expand the talks beyond the existing Russian, Ukrainian and US delegations. No date had been agreed for the next round, he added.
European governments, meanwhile, were preparing their negotiating team while maintaining pressure on Moscow.
Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee welcomed renewed talks and the agreement on EU representation following diplomatic meetings in Abu Dhabi and Dublin last week. But she said, “Russia has clearly not changed its position.”
Speaking ahead of Monday’s meeting of EU foreign ministers in Brussels, McEntee said 113 new sanctions on Russia were intended to maintain pressure on Moscow “as it intensified attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure during the winter”.
“We are also working to ensure Ukraine has the finance and the military support it needs while advancing Ukraine’s path to EU membership,” she said.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Russia wanted a lasting peace rather than a temporary ceasefire that would allow Ukraine to recover from the damage inflicted by Russian forces.
He said Moscow sought peace lasting “years, even centuries”, adding that negotiations were complex and could take considerable time.
Separately, Trump said he would discuss the war with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin in China, saying he believed Putin wanted to end the war.
“I think he’s backing down a little bit,” Trump told reporters. “Frankly, I think he’d like to see it finish.”
The planned Berlin meeting would allow Ukraine and its supporters to agree on their next negotiating steps. Russia had yet to accept their proposed representation in the talks that would follow.

Wales take on Portugal in the Nations League on Tuesday, with the visitors without Cristiano Ronaldo in Cardiff after his retirement; Ben Davies is pretty pleased the legendary forward is not in the Portugal squad - with Craig Bellamy unmoved by the whole saga
The Cardiff City Stadium sold out very quickly when the Nations League fixtures threw up a Wales vs Portugal game for the final match of Group D.
Mark the date, November 17, 2026 - it could have been the last time to see Cristiano Ronaldo play on UK soil.
A mouthwatering occasion to witness one of the greats of the game as the curtain slowly falls on his illustrious international career and also see just how far Wales are progressing after a full campaign in League A of the Nations League, a full campaign among the heavyweights of European football.
As we all know, that's not how it's panned out! After Ronaldo's appearance against Wales in Lisbon at the start of the Nations League, he's not featured since - and he's now called time on his Portugal career amid some controversy.
Even though Ronaldo's not here in Wales and the ending of his Portugal days were perhaps not the best scripted, he'll certainly be missed by many. Wales manager Craig Bellamy for one: "As soon as he retires then suddenly like, it's all hell breaks loose!
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player
"He is one of the best players that has ever played the game. We are all going to miss him. Now, he's still playing club football, so we still get little bits to watch him.
"So just be grateful you got to see an incredible talent that you can call yours, and this is me speaking to Portuguese people. But I'm grateful that we got to see the longevity of a true great, who's had one of the biggest impacts in football in general and will go on to have a big impact by just the young kids who watch him.
"I feel it's like stop the talking now. Just celebrate. Celebrate. I'm grateful I got to see him and I'm grateful I got to coach against him as well."
Wales captain Ben Davies offered a wry smile and an alternative view of Ronaldo's retirement, from an opposition player's perspective: "Any game where you probably don't play against Cristiano Ronaldo, I think it's sometimes better for you…" That's Davies at his most understated!
He added: "You're not too concerned of what he can do to you on that day, he's a world-class player. It's been an honour and a privilege to share the pitch with him because of what he's done in the game. We were lucky to do that in Lisbon, but there won't be too many players in Wales complaining that he's not going to be there."
Despite the Wales-Portugal fixture having implications for both countries, more questions were asked about Ronaldo than perhaps most others. Welsh, British and Portuguese reporters were all guilty at some point of asking media questions about the missing No 7.
Take away the circus that followed and still follows Ronaldo, so many Wales fans thought about buying a ticket and coming along to watch Ronaldo strut his stuff and to also show their appreciation, that it's actually difficult to ignore Ronaldo's absence from their perspective.
Fans pay good money to watch elite sport and many had hoped a farewell to Ronaldo was part of the entrance fee. A great shame for nigh on 35,000 inside the Cardiff City Stadium on Tuesday night.
What the crowd will get though is a Portugal side packed with talent - the quality and depth of their squad on paper is ridiculous.
But it's a squad that has come to Cardiff slightly reeling from a very unexpected home thrashing at the hands of Denmark who beat them 4-1 at the weekend.
Is this what Portugal will be like without Ronaldo? I doubt it… but Wales have a free shot at Portugal, their League A campaign has only mustered one win, but bar a drab home game against Denmark, Bellamy's side have gone toe to toe with Portugal and Norway.
There have been "moments" as Bellamy ruefully alluded to in all matches where Wales have produced quality and consistency beyond their opponents. It's brought a victory over Norway, but in the other four games Wales have just been short. Short, but at least trying.
Even the most ardent Wales supporter who is not a "Bellamy" fans (and there a few) can't talk away some plain stats. Wales have enjoyed decent possession in all their League A games and create chances - 12 against Norway last Saturday. Perhaps one link missing is an out and out goalscorer where chances created and shots at goal actually turn into 'goals'.
For Bellamy this League A campaign has been fruitful IF you can look beyond the short term: "You want to be exposed to the profile of teams we've been exposed to. It's beyond motivating to play these teams and even the moments that don't go your way, you learn, you know? Like that killer moment.
"You can't get away with anything, can you? At the moment, we've got in, we're side-netting (not the goal), so it's the difference. I thought we definitely brought a good version of ourselves to these games, we've definitely been competitive in these games and I expect us to be competitive, but it's just final moments, those final details.
"Are we creating opportunities to score? Well, xG is higher than what we're converging so that's telling you we're creating big opportunities.
"They're the moments that can turn what you feel is a good performance into actually coming away and winning these type of games and I believe the best way you're able to do that is by playing against them on a regular basis, by being in that position.
"So yeah, we're desperate to stay in Group A. We want to stay in this league, it motivates us a lot to stay in this league."
Bellamy's Wales will finish bottom of their group, but their record is better than many other teams in League A such as Czech Republic, Serbia and Turkey so they will not be automatically relegated.
A play-off awaits Wales next March against a League B runner-up. Wales will take that and fancy their chances especially with the home leg second.
With Euro 2028 the longer term aim, remaining in League A the medium term aim, the short term is to do a Wales 'rugby'.
Defy the pundits and 'superior' opposition and create a result and performance that many people talk about for years to come and say to one another; "I was there… even if Ronaldo wasn't."
