Declan Rice has agreed a new long term-contract at Arsenal so can he continue to go from strength to strength? Jack Wilshere, his former team-mate at West Ham, tells Sky Sports Rice is "definitely in the conversation as one of the best midfielders in the world"
Arsenal's Kroenke family owners tend not to get involved in transfer dealings but when it came to Declan Rice, and the prospect of spending £100m on a player for the first time, they needed to be sure that it was a sensible investment.
So, in the conference room at Arsenal's training ground, co-chair Josh Kroenke asked to be walked through the deal by Mikel Arteta, former sporting director Edu, then executive vice-chair Tim Lewis and now chief executive officer Richard Garlick.
"My eyebrows raised because I didn't know if we were in that phase just yet to go after a player like that," Kroenke recalled. He wanted to know what he would bring and how Arteta would use him. He wanted reassurance that he could hit the ground running.
Kroenke left the meeting in no doubt about the deal, either financially or in footballing terms. A club-record approach to West Ham was greenlit and Rice has of course gone on to prove an inspired addition, his new deal reflecting his importance.
"Declan Rice, we got him half price," is the refrain among Arsenal supporters. A player instrumental in their Premier League title success, who insisted "it's not done" then did more than anyone to drive them over the line, is now tied down for his peak years.
He has brought Arsenal even more than the club anticipated, arriving as a No 6 before being unshackled as a rampaging No 8, then reverting to a deeper role this season.
He scores, creates and dominates physically. His deadly set-piece delivery is another string to his bow.
"He is becoming a total player," said Arteta, who has even called on him at right-back. Of course, Rice filled in admirably in that role. "A total player has to be able to do as many things as possible and he has the capacity to do that," added Arteta.
Rice's adaptability and willingness to evolve his game have been themes of his time at Arsenal and the same traits were apparent to those who worked with him at West Ham, where he made an instant impression on his former team-mate Jack Wilshere.
"I love Declan, first of all a person," Wilshere tells Sky Sports. "I could see that straight away when I went in. He was very humble, his eyes were open, he wanted to learn, he would ask the right questions, and he just went from strength to strength.
"His footballing ability speaks for itself, but I wouldn't say he's someone who it came naturally to. He had to work on his right foot, on his left foot. But physically, he was always a beast and that would help him get out of certain situations."
Wilshere also noted the leadership qualities that have come to the fore at Arsenal. "Even when I went there and he was 19 or 20 and finding his way in the team, he had natural leadership and a natural aura about him that you could see," he says.
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player
"He has a good understanding as well. When you look at players making big moves now, for me, one of the most important things around it is timing. I think Dec got his timing right.
"He spent a good few years at West Ham becoming a hero, becoming an important member of that team, trying to get that team up the table to finish high as possible. He won a trophy with them, and then he decided to go and compete for bigger things."
Wilshere and Rice crossed paths again following his move to Arsenal, where Wilshere, now head coach of Luton Town, was working as an academy coach and shadowing his old team-mate Arteta.
"I know how important he was to Mikel at that time when Mikel brought him in, and how he was going to be that shining light of the team who would always be present," he says.
"That's another thing that's really impressive about him: his robustness. He plays every single game. He dominates every single game physically."
Rice's record bears it out. Last season was his most demanding yet as he made 55 appearances in all competitions for Arsenal, many of them while managing hamstring nerve pain, before making a further eight for England at the World Cup during the summer.
He is an incredible athlete who continues to show remarkable resistance to injury. He has only missed five out of 119 Premier League games since his arrival at Arsenal. Only four outfield players have played more minutes in the competition in that timeframe.
His reliability is invaluable to Arteta and Rice continues to find ways to improve. Having moved back to the base of midfield this term, switching to the right side of the pivot to accommodate Myles Lewis-Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes, he has become notably more incisive with his passes.
According to Opta, Rice ranks second among Premier League players - and top among midfielders - for line-breaking passes this season, behind only Jan Paul van Hecke. He also ranks second only to Martin Odegaard for line-breaking passes in the final third.
He is sometimes criticised for sideways passing but he is averaging nearly twice as many line-breaking passes than last season, showing clear development in yet another area of his game.
The hope for Arsenal is that Rice will continue to unlock more levels after committing his future to the club. And certainly, that is the expectation from those who know him.
"I actually think there's more to come from Dec," adds Wilshere. "I've said it for a few years now. To be fair, he has started to add goals, but I still think he can add more with his physical ability, with his ability to strike the ball off his left foot, right foot.
"But he's already a top player and definitely in the conversation as one of the best midfielders in the world."

By supporting the non-profit BigShoe, the Arsenal forward has earned deserved plaudits for his social conscience
V alerie Fiesser will never forget her surprise when Bukayo Saka contacted her out of the blue, asking whether he could help support a project in Nigeria in 2022. “I remember thinking: ‘Is this really Bukayo writing us an email?’” says the president of BigShoe, a non-profit organisation based in Frankfurt that has helped more than 10,000 children worldwide. “But that’s how he is. He’s always asking what more we can do.”
Four years on from that unexpected email, Fiesser was given the secret task of reaching out for a letter for Saka to read from the podium when he was presented with the Sócrates award at last month’s Ballon d’Or ceremony in London for his humanitarian work. She got the words from Byiringiro, a 14-year-old from Rwanda who had his eyesight restored after having surgery thanks to BigShoe’s initiative.
“They told me he was going to receive the award, but he didn’t know, so they asked whether I could get a letter from one of the children we had helped,” Fiesser says. “I was really proud of Bukayo, I think the way he did it was really special. He stood there so strongly for all these children around the world that nobody sees and nobody hears. He gave them a voice. He took the attention away from himself and put it into action. That’s how I know Bukayo. It’s never about him, it’s always about the people we help. He’s incredible.”
Saka, who donated more than 1,000 school uniforms to children in his home borough of Ealing in west London last year to help with the cost of living crisis, is understood to have heard about BigShoe from Antonio Rüdiger after the Real Madrid and Germany defender told him about some of the work he had done with the organisation in Africa. It has also worked with Philipp Lahm and Mesut Özil in the past. Fiesser says Saka and his family have taken a particularly close interest in which projects he supports.
“When we had 150 life-changing surgeries taking place in Nigeria, he would message me asking to see pictures. He wanted to know what was happening and whether everybody was safe. He always asks whether the team has returned safely. I don’t know how he manages to find the time, but he does. His family are very similar. They genuinely want to make a big impact and provide meaningful help. I wouldn’t describe Bukayo as simply a donor to BigShoe. He’s more like a member of the BigShoe team. I know that he stands behind us.”
BigShoe was established by four friends in 2006 after the World Cup. As part of its latest projects in Rwanda and Nigeria, about 3,000 people had eye examinations and were provided with glasses if required. “Giving a child a pair of glasses can change their life,” Fiesser says. “We also help entire families. If a father can’t see properly, he might not be able to work or read. That affects the whole family.”
BigShoe recently renovated a school in Rwanda and provided clean drinking water through a water filtration system. It has also built a library and provided private changing facilities for girls. “Once a month, some girls miss school because they don’t have suitable facilities or somewhere private to change,” says Fiesser. “We built facilities so they can continue attending school and have a quiet, private area.”
Saka’s hectic playing schedule means he has yet to make a visit but his family have been on the ground in Rwanda and he was heavily involved in funding earthquake relief projects in Morocco and Turkey. “We provided container homes for people affected by the earthquakes,” says Fiesser. “I knew I could count on him. It’s always important to Bukayo that we make a big impact. He doesn’t want money to be wasted. When I present a project to him, he wants to understand it properly. He needs to know exactly what we’re doing before he makes a decision. He’s a 100% person. Whatever he does, he gives it everything.”
Saka’s mother, Adenike, is believed to be a driving force behind her son’s charitable work, with Fiesser describing her as “one of the most amazing women I’ve met”. Plans are being made for the next projects, which include providing health insurance to families in Nigeria and food packages for children in Rwanda over Christmas.
“He doesn’t just want to give someone food,” Fiesser says. “Of course, food is important, and we’re providing that too, but he wants to change lives. You can help someone, but if the help doesn’t last, then it hasn’t achieved what you really wanted. If we all work together, it doesn’t matter which team we’re supporting or which country we’re helping. We’re all part of one world.”

Declan Rice has just over 18 months left on his existing contract, with a further year's option in Arsenal's favour; the Premier League champions want to bring him in line with the club's top earner, Bukayo Saka; Rice admitted on England duty that he is close to a new agreement
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player
Declan Rice has verbally agreed terms on a new long-term contract at Arsenal, Sky Sports News can reveal.
Sky Sports News has been told his new deal will bring him in line with Bukayo Saka, who is the highest-paid player at the Emirates.
Rice and his representatives have been in negotiations for several months, with the club keen to tie down one of their most important players, even though he still has 18 months left on his existing contract, with a further year's option in the club's favour.
Rice was named Arsenal's Player of the Year last season when they won the Premier League title and this new deal will take him into his early 30s.
The 27-year-old joined Arsenal from West Ham for a club record £105m in 2023. He's gone on to be a key member of Mikel Arteta's leadership group, and someone who the Spanish coach has built his team around.
Speaking on Saturday ahead of England's final Nations League group game in Spain, Rice confirmed that he was close to an agreement.
"I'm a player that always sets myself targets, always pushes for more. I've always been stable in the clubs I'm at. The new contract is hopefully on the horizon soon.
"I'm extremely lucky I'm at a club like Arsenal where the manager shows me so much trust. I've so many team-mates who put so much energy and effort into me. I'm extremely lucky that I don't have to worry about that stuff. It makes playing football a lot easier."
Arsenal are not just tying down Declan Rice - one of their most important players - to a bumper new deal, they are tying down arguably the Premier League's best player into his remaining peak years.
And this season is the best version we've ever seen from Rice.
The England midfielder has started the campaign on fire and tops the Premier League assist charts at the moment with five - all of them from open play.
But this creative spark from Rice has come despite the Arsenal man playing a deeper role in Mikel Arteta's set-up. A sitting midfielder, yes - but still as attacking as ever.
No midfielder in the Premier League has made more final third passes or passes through the lines than Rice this season.
His number of final third entries has nearly doubled compared to two seasons ago. And his recent goal for Arsenal against Bayern Munich in the Champions League summed up how he is influencing the top end of the pitch a lot more.
That goal cancelled out Harry Kane's strike for Bayern. Rice is Arsenal's superstar equivalent.
Rice can do everything in midfield for Arsenal. He can hurt teams by running through them, or passing through the lines. He can score, as well as create. He can damage from open play, or from his deadly delivery from corners and free-kicks. He is the complete midfielder.
Meanwhile, another huge figure in the Arsenal starting XI - captain Martin Odegaard - has said he has not yet begun negotiations over a new contract, even though his current deal expires at the same time as Rice's.
Speaking while on international duty with Norway, the Arsenal captain said: "I'm happy and hope I can be there for a long time to come, but so far we haven't started on that.
"There is no stress about it. I am where I am, and I am super happy with it. Things are going well, and it is not something I am stressed about. As I said, I want to be there for a long time to come. I am enjoying myself a lot."

‘We will not go back on this way of playing,’ says Thomas Tuchel after he delivered response to World Cup critics
T homas Tuchel made defensive substitutions as England protected a lead. He finished with three centre-backs on the pitch. His team could not get out of their half in the final part of the game. So close your eyes and imagine an alternate universe in which James Trafford did not make his stunning double save in stoppage time on Sunday and England had drawn 3-3 with Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium rather than won 3-2 . The reaction would not have been kind because Tuchel has been here before.
The head coach wanted to push one particular comparison from the World Cup over the summer. “It was Mexico reloaded,” he said, with a nod towards the 3-2 last-16 win at the Azteca Stadium and it fitted like a glove – down to the detail of Jarell Quansah and red cards.
Against Mexico, the defender was sent off for a late tackle in the 54th minute with England 2-1 up. Against Spain, he contributed to Elliot Anderson being sent off in the 63rd minute with England 3-0 up. Quansah had his pocket picked by Lamine Yamal and Anderson’s attempt to chase back and rectify the situation ended with him fouling the winger.
It was not only a red card but a penalty; the prompt for Spain to launch a furious and hitherto unadvertised fightback. It had the stand that housed the press box shaking. Structural integrity was very much a theme.
As in Mexico, Tuchel made defensive changes. This time, it was Myles Lewis-Skelly for Harry Kane; Djed Spence for Anthony Gordon. Tuchel also withdrew Jude Bellingham, who went off shaking his head. It was easy to understand his frustration. He was excellent. Tuchel had removed his two prime attackers. He also put Dan Burn on towards the end, albeit this time not as part of a back five. England stayed in a 4-4-1 formation, with Quansah moving from central defence to right-back. As in Mexico, the 10-man low block resisted.
As much as Tuchel disagreed, this felt like Argentina reloaded as well. “No, not at all,” he said, when the World Cup semi-final defeat was raised. “Because of one man down. We would not have been in this situation if it was 11 against 11.”
The parallels, nevertheless, were there. Tuchel made defensive substitutions at 1-0 up against Argentina; it was a back five on that occasion. As against Spain, his team could not get out and they faced a flurry of chances. There were other factors in play at the World Cup, chief among them the high levels of fatigue within the squad. England could not hold out, conceding two late goals to exit and bring down a wave of criticism on Tuchel.
The score is the ultimate takeaway. It can skew analysis. Had Trafford not got back up after parrying a shot from the Spain substitute Fermín López to brilliantly repel Aymeric Laporte’s follow‑up, England would have gone from enjoying a fabulous result to stewing over an opportunity missed. The stakes were nowhere near as high as at the World Cup, but they would have gone from finishing top of their Nations League group to advancing into the quarter-finals as an unseeded second-place team.
In terms of Tuchel’s approach to the closing stages of a big game, what changed?
The truth for England lay in the opening 63 minutes. This was where the evidence of a decisive shift could be found, the reasons for the swell of optimism . England have never played better under Tuchel – and this was against the team to beat; the world and European champions. On their turf.
Spain were without the injured Rodri and Dani Olmo, and Luis de la Fuente strangely decided to use Pedri only as a substitute, but their lineup still shimmered with menace; Lamine Yamal was frightening. Yet before their penalty, converted by Mikel Oyarzabal, they did not have a shot on target. Or a real chance.
What stood out from the first whistle was England’s front‑foot intent; the bravery on the ball. They believed they would win and there was a fearlessness about them. They made forward moves on the half turn. There was a slickness about their combinations.
Spain have never suffered like this under De la Fuente and it was everything Tuchel had dreamed of when he started to plot a new version of his team after the World Cup; a more fluid game model, a response to the Argentina defeat.
Tuchel loved England’s buildup play , which included some of Trafford’s passing. He loved the high press; the aggression in the duels; the threat on set pieces. He said he loved the low-block defending too. Ben White was excellent at right-back and there was a coming-of-age performance from Lewis Hall at left-back, but it felt wrong to single out individuals.
“We didn’t stop and I think we are ready to go [like this] for 90 minutes,” Tuchel said. “It was a complete performance and we will not look back now. Go forward and stay hungry. We will not go back on this way of playing that we find ourselves since the World Cup.”
Ezri Konsa, who headed in the second goal from a Declan Rice corner, said England “would have scored two more” if they had kept 11 men on the pitch. “You saw until the red card how much quality we had,” he said.
“We dominated the game. The instruction was to keep going at them. Don’t stop. To keep our foot on the pedal. Argentina was different; different circumstances.”
Tuchel was asked about the journey from the heartbreak of Argentina to this point; the end of a stirring Nations League group campaign, including the 7-0 win against Croatia in Rijeka. It has not all been super exciting; the 2-1 Wembley win against Croatia last Thursday, for example, was a grind. Was he always confident of a successful reboot?
“It took me a while to digest [the World Cup] and see the way forward,” he said. “How we can help and adjust and improve? We had reviews and so on but the clarity came in the first Nations League camp [in September and October] with the players.
“The first week was not so easy. Some players were still upset from the World Cup. Some were new in the team. Some had digested it, some had not. But it was important to have this process together and everyone committed to wanting to improve in certain aspects of the game.
“We had the energy right to take the next steps and from there we went. Full credit to the players, how they buy in. It’s amazing that it came together like this now.”

Soren Colding wasn't expecting the call. "The Laudrup brothers, Peter Schmeichel, there might have been some cancellations," he jokes.
Eventually, the Danish FA turned to a Brondby defender who had played a handful of times for the national team.
The assignment? He would be expected to mark Ronaldo and Gabriel Batistuta as part of a Europe XI against the Rest of the World at Marseille's Velodrome.
It was December 1997, and Colding's team-mates would include defenders Fernando Hierro and Alessandro Costacurta, a midfield duo of Zinedine Zidane and Paul Ince, and Patrick Kluivert and Alen Boksic up top.
This was a star-sprinkled cast - one player from each of the competing nations at the following summer's World Cup joining forces before the draw took place.
"Of course, when you see those names, it was just more or less a dream come true," explains the Dane.
Colding was flown to France and chauffeured to the hotel. His driver offered to hang around in case the full-back fancied an impromptu shopping trip. There was no need. Instead, he discovered a bag of Fifa goodies in his room.
"There was the biggest Adidas bag I have ever seen in my life," he smiles. "I found a training suit and went down to lunch.
"Then I saw all the other guys on round tables - they were sitting with their agents, their wives, their family, their friends in normal [clothes]. Then the Danish guy turned in. Nobody knows who he is, in his Adidas training suit!"
Colding struck up a friendship with South Africa defender David Nyathi and the pair where whisked off to a 45-minute training session that afternoon. Not all the big names took part, but one Argentine offered a taste of what was to come.
"Batistuta was there and just to see him and his moves, you thought, 'Okay, it's gonna be a nice evening tomorrow'," remembers Colding, who also got to link up with European boss Franz Beckenbauer.
"He was pretty cool. He was saying, 'what is your position? Defender? OK, can you play left defender?' No problem - I'll play wherever you place me!"
Ronaldo scored twice and assisted three more goals as Rest of the World beat their Europe counterparts 5-2 in Marseille
Come game day, 38,000 fans packed in to see peak Ronaldo. Months earlier, Il Fenomeno completed a world-record move to Inter Milan on the back of 47 goals in 49 games in one sensational season at Barcelona.
"It was crazy, actually," recalls Colding, who previously faced the forward when Denmark's under-21s played Brazil in Florianopolis before the 1996 Olympics.
"That was almost the same team as they played with at the World Cup in '98. So we lost 5-1. Just to see his speed and how he played - I played against Roberto Carlos in that game as well - that was just another level. I thought, 'what is going on here?'
"When I saw him there again, it was just to see what is actually reachable for a football player, because that was next level tremendous. His speed and his touch are unbelievable, and also his power.
"And still, just a small, shy guy. You know, he just wants to play football, and all these people are around him protecting him. Just to see when a star like him joins an event like that, how many people around him, agents and followers, how should you navigate all that?"
Ronaldo, captaining Carlos Alberto Parreira's side, was at his blistering best, scoring twice and setting up the other three as Rest of the World won 5-2 - Batistuta also netted twice, before Zidane responded.
"You start thinking what if you injured some of them," explains Colding. "You are a defender, you don't want goals against you, so you have to fight - that's how I am.
"How hard should you go to them? Should you just let them go? No. I would not just let them run and score. I tried to do my best, that was probably not good enough!"
Diego Maradona featured for a Rest of the World XI in August 1987 - a year after Argentina beat England at the World Cup
This wasn't the first outing for a World XI, in fact such Fifa exhibition matches had been taking place since England hosted an all-star side in front of a reported 100,000 fans at Wembley in 1963 to celebrate the Football Association's centenary.
They became a semi-regular occurrence as testimonials or charity fixtures, with huge names appearing across eras from Eusebio and Zico to Roberto Baggio.
But the biggest coup was arguably luring Diego Maradona to Wembley a year after winning the World Cup with Argentina and scoring his 'Hand of God' goal against England.
Jon Smith, who represented the Napoli star, explains in his book 'The Deal' how Maradona was offered around £250,000 and flown from Naples on a private jet to take part in an anniversary game against the Football League.
"In fairness, he wanted to shake hands with the team and say 'sorry if I offended you'," Smith tells BBC Sport. "He genuinely believed his talent was God-given.
"He was sort of two people. He was lovely, Diego, when you were with him. When he crossed the white line he was Maradona. So the Hand of God was an expression of 'I am God's footballing representative', if you like.
"It was madness, because you can imagine how the media were all over it. It was a bit special."
Napoli and Argentina welcomed the opportunity for Maradona to generate some good PR in England, helped by Bobby Robson's Football League side winning 3-0 - Bryan Robson netting twice and Norman Whiteside grabbing the other.
"I remember introducing him to Bobby Robson," adds Smith. "He put his hand out, and Bobby said 'I'm not shaking that hand!', which I thought was lovely - he did shake the other hand!"
A Ronaldinho XI beat their Shevchenko counterparts 6-3 in February 2005 - Ronaldinho, Samuel Eto'o, Alessandro Del Piero and Gianfranco Zola were all on the scoresheet
One of the final games saw a Ronaldinho XI take on a Shevchenko XI at Nou Camp in February 2005 to raise funds for victims of the 2004 tsunami.
Andriy Shevchenko's stacked squad included Zidane, David Beckham, Alessandro Del Piero, Thierry Henry, Raul, Paolo Maldini and Steven Gerrard.
Ronaldinho could call on Ronaldo, Kaka, Cafu, Adriano, Javier Zanetti, Didier Drogba and Samuel Eto'o, though it was Southampton's Henri Camara who scored twice in a 6-3 win for the Brazilian's team.
But things have moved on, and it is hard to imagine clubs releasing their star players for such an exhibition nowadays.
"The whole world of football has changed," says Smith. "You used to have testimonial games and testimonial years because players got paid okay but by the same token weren't earning £100k a week.
"It wouldn't happen now because the business of football is so much bigger, you can't risk the players - if they get injured playing for their country, that annoys everybody.
"But beyond that they are owned by big corporations and in some cases countries, so you just wouldn't allow your player to go out and do that."
Colding went on to play 27 times for Denmark, featuring at the 1998 World Cup and Euro 2000, but retains fond memories of representing the Europe XI.
"Now, to come up with the idea to make a game like this, in combination with the draw, I think everyone will say you are crazy," explains Colding.
"But at that time it was perfectly planned and a fantastic event to be a part of. As players, we have a tremendous relationship between each other.
"It shows all the spectators you can be enemies on the field, but you can actually be friends and gather together in this kind of event.
"That for me sends a signal to all that we are a community in football and we can actually make great things together that not only is a question of money."
In fact, he still has his Europe shirt - a reminder of coming up against Ronaldo and Batistuta and being a team-mate of Zidane almost 30 years ago.
"It doesn't smell very good, actually," laughs Colding. "Sometimes, when I go in the garage with my kids and tell them about it and what actually happened, I see in their eyes, they don't really believe that I was a part of that game.

Seeking redemption after failing at Spurs, newly installed Crystal Palace manager has a tough challenge ahead
T homas Frank promised his wife, Nanna, he would take a year’s sabbatical after being sacked by Tottenham in February , but he couldn’t wait that long. Having received a reported £8m payoff from Spurs, he kept an extremely low profile in the first few months after an experience at the club that sources close to the 53‑year‑old have described as “traumatic”.
Frank broke his silence at the start of June with a statement released by the League Managers Association. It said he would cover the World Cup for the BBC (thereby going head-to-head with Ange Postecoglou, his predecessor at Spurs, who worked for ITV) before “experiencing the Tour de France”, a lifelong passion. Frank usually preferred to run to Brentford’s training ground and home matches from his home in East Sheen during a nine‑year spell as assistant and then manager, but he occasionally cycled because it helped to clear his head.
By the time the statement was released the Crystal Palace chair, Steve Parish, is understood to have sounded out Frank out over his willingness to take over from Oliver Glasner . But it confirmed his intention to keep his promise and not rush back into management. “When the time is right, I will look forward to my return as a manager, ready to embrace the job with great energy and dedication,” he said.
With Palace facing the prospect of ending a 14-season stay in the Premier League – the eighth‑longest in the division – after a dreadful start under Pierre Sage , that time has arrived. Frank left Tottenham with a win ratio of 34.2% – the worst of any permanent manager in the club’s history – but has the chance to redeem himself at a club he is said to have admired from afar.
According to the biography Thomas Frank: The Premier League Diaries, by the Danish author Kasper Steenbach, published last year, Frank attended the 2025 FA Cup final victory against Manchester City with a childhood friend from Denmark who supports Palace after arranging tickets for him. Frank is said to have been impressed by the atmosphere for which Selhurst Park has become renowned. That said, the absence of the influential supporters’ group the Holmesdale Fanatics since it disbanded at the start of the season has made it less intimidating for visiting teams.
Nonetheless, Frank is said to be itching to return to the dugout after failing at Spurs, where he inherited a squad that had just won the Europa League under Postecoglou but struggled to impose himself at a club with higher expectations. Frank’s preference to play on the counterattack with a more direct style looks a better fit at Palace, although his critics will question whether his success at Brentford was really down to the system put in place by the club’s owner, Matthew Benham, that has allowed Keith Andrews to thrive since the former set-piece coach stepped into Frank’s shoes.
There is no such framework in place at Palace, with their longevity in the Premier League mainly down to a series of shrewd managerial appointments at the right time by Parish which have ensured they have not finished lower than 15th since being promoted in 2013. Frank, who is also understood to have attracted interest from Denmark in the summer and Newcastle and Fulham in recent weeks after difficult starts for Matthias Jaissle and Álvaro Arbeloa respectively, will be expected to make an immediate impression.
For now he must make do with a squad seriously lacking in leaders after the sales of Marc Guéhi, Maxence Lacroix and Daniel Muñoz this year. Frank’s first task must be to instil some defensive discipline in a side who have conceded 24 goals in 10 league games.
His Brentford side were renowned for their organisation and prowess from set pieces, an area Palace have struggled with for several seasons. He will have to tread carefully if he intends to impose the “no dickheads” policy he borrowed from the All Blacks during his time as Brentford manager.
Sage’s attempts to impose himself on the squad by dropping the defenders Jaydee Canvot and Axel Disasi for poor performances and indiscipline respectively backfired because his team kept losing, not to mention that it angered Parish . Frank, who is believed to have been offered assurances that Palace will bring in defensive reinforcements in January, faces a delicate balancing act with a squad desperately low on morale.
The futures of Ismaïla Sarr and Jean‑Philippe Mateta could be key to Palace’s prospects of avoiding the drop. Sarr was the club’s player of the year when they won the Conference League last season but he played only 107 minutes in the Premier League under Sage owing to a groin injury. The Senegal forward’s head was turned by interest from Liverpool in the summer and Frank will have to rely on his best motivational skills to get the best out of him and Mateta, who is suspended for crucial games against Coventry and Hull after his red card against Tottenham .
The France striker tried to annul the final year of his contract after a move to Milan was scuppered by a failed medical in January and he is likely to push for a move again. But he remains popular in the dressing room and could be the talisman for Palace’s survival push if Frank can persuade him that the grass may not be greener.

1999 yılında Magazin Gazetecileri Derneği'nin ödül töreninde Ahmet Kaya 'ya yönelik gerçekleştirilen protesto, yıllar geçmesine rağmen tartışılmaya devam ediyor. O gece 10. Yıl Marşı'na eşlik ettiği için eleştirilen şarkıcı Mahsun Kırmızıgül, yaptığı son açıklamayla yeniden gündeme geldi.
Kırmızıgül, o gece ayağa kalkmasının Ahmet Kaya 'ya tepki göstermek amacı taşımadığını belirterek yaşananları farklı bir açıdan değerlendirdi. Salonda ayağa kalkmaması halinde kendisinin de ağır tepkilerle karşılaşabileceğini söyleyen Kırmızıgül, "O salonda ayağa kalkmasaydım başıma neler geleceğini, nasıl bir linçle karşı karşıya kalacağımı bugün bile düşünemiyorum" dedi.
Ahmet Kaya 'nın Türkiye'den ayrılmasına neden olan sürecin sorumluluğunun yalnızca o gece salonda bulunan kişilere yüklenemeyeceğini savunan Kırmızıgül, asıl sorumluluğun dönemin medyası ve siyasi atmosferinde olduğunu ifade etti. Kaya ile arasında yaşanan kırgınlığa da değinen ünlü şarkıcı, yeniden görüşmek için Almanya'ya gitmeyi düşündüğünü ancak Kaya'nın bir konserinde söylediği iddia edilen sözleri duyduktan sonra bu kararından vazgeçtiğini anlattı. Bu kararından dolayı pişmanlık duyduğunu belirten Kırmızıgül, "Keşke gitseydim. Keşke oturup konuşsaydık. Keşke birbirimizi dinleyebilseydik" ifadelerini kullandı.
Ahmet Kaya 'nın vefatının ardından Paris'e giderek mezarı başında vedalaştığını söyleyen Kırmızıgül, hakkındaki eleştirilere ise şu sözlerle yanıt verdi: "Ben hiçbir zaman Ahmet Kaya 'ya düşman olmadım. Onu protesto etmedim. Ona yapılan saldırının ve linçin hiçbir zaman parçası olmadım."
Kırmızıgül'ün son açıklamalarının ardından, yıllar önce Reha Muhtar'ın programına konuk olduğu sırada Ahmet Kaya hakkında yaptığı değerlendirmeler de yeniden gündeme geldi. Programda yaşananları "Yanlış bir geceydi" sözleriyle değerlendiren Kırmızıgül, Ahmet Kaya'nın açıklamalarına ilişkin dikkat çeken ifadeler kullanmıştı. Kırmızıgül, o programda, "Yanlış bir geceydi. O gece bunların olmaması gerekirdi. Ahmet Kaya, söylediklerini farklı bir dille söylese bugün böyle olmayabilirdi. Kürtçe zaten şu anda serbest... Binlerce Kürtçe kaset var" demişti.

Düğün sırasında şarkıcıya para takmak isteyen bir davetlinin davranışı gerginliğe neden oldu. Davetliye sert sözlerle seslenen şarkıcı, "Kendine gel, her yerde şımarıklık yapma. Haddini bil, haddini bil. Burada 5 bin som verip istediğim işi yaptırırım deme, anladın mı?" ifadelerini kullandı.
